records.content:
Section 6.4.4 left an open question: on separable data the logistic regression without a penalty has no minimizer, the weights diverge, and “the unpenalized fit is determined by the stopping rule”. We can now say what the stopping rule does. Take labels y_i \in \{-1, +1\}, features \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i (with a constant coordinate for the intercept), and suppose that some \mathbf{w} has y_i\mathbf{w}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i > 0 for all i. The hard-margin direction is the solution of\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}}\ \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert \quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i\,\mathbf{w}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i \ge 1\ \text{ for all } i,

the separating hyperplane with the largest margin, the object of Chapter 8.

Theorem 7.14 (implicit bias of gradient descent; Soudry et al., 2018; stated without proof)

For linearly separable data, gradient descent on the unpenalized logistic loss with a constant step \eta < 2/L, from any starting point, satisfies f(\mathbf{w}_k) \to 0, \lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVert \to \infty, and\frac{\mathbf{w}_k}{\lVert\mathbf{w}_k\rVert} \longrightarrow \frac{\hat{\mathbf{w}}}{\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert},
\qquad
\mathbf{w}_k = \hat{\mathbf{w}}\,\ln k + \boldsymbol\rho_k,

where the correction \boldsymbol\rho_k grows much more slowly than \ln k (it is bounded when the support vectors span the data). The direction converges only at the rate O(1/\ln k).

In words: the logistic loss decreases forever by growing the weights, the size of \mathbf{w}_k is set by the number of iterations (logarithmically), and the direction converges, among all the separating directions, to the one with the largest margin. Early stopping then chooses a size, hence how confident the probabilities are, while the direction is already that of the support vector machine. Worked example 7.2 was the one-dimensional case: w_k grows like \log k.

We check the theorem on the two Iris classes of Section 6.4.4 (setosa against versicolor, petal length and width, standardized), which are separable. We append the constant column and compute the hard-margin direction in the augmented space with LinearSVC with a very large C, without intercept: that is the optimization problem above (we use it here as a black box, and Chapter 8 explains it). Then we run gradient descent with \eta = 1/L for one million iterations and compare.

iris = load_iris()
mask = iris.target < 2
Zi = StandardScaler().fit_transform(iris.data[mask][:, [2, 3]])
yi = iris.target[mask].astype(float)                          # 0 = setosa, 1 = versicolor
Ai = np.c_[np.ones(len(yi)), Zi]                               # augmented features
si = 2 * yi - 1                                                # labels in {-1, +1}

svm = LinearSVC(C=1e6, loss="hinge", fit_intercept=False, dual=True, max_iter=2_000_000, tol=1e-10).fit(Ai, yi)
w_hat = svm.coef_.ravel()
margins = si * (Ai @ w_hat)
print(f"hard-margin direction (augmented space): {np.round(w_hat, 4)}, ||w_hat|| = {np.linalg.norm(w_hat):.4f}")
print(f"constraints that are active (margin = 1): examples {np.flatnonzero(margins < 1 + 1e-6)}; "
      f"largest geometric margin = 1/||w_hat|| = {1 / np.linalg.norm(w_hat):.4f}")

L_i = np.linalg.eigvalsh(Ai.T @ Ai / len(yi))[-1] / 4
w_i = np.zeros(3)
checkpoints = {10, 100, 1000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000}
rows, path_i = [], []
log_ks = set(np.unique(np.round(np.logspace(0, 6, 61)).astype(int)))
for k in range(1, 1_000_001):
    w_i = w_i - (1 / L_i) * (Ai.T @ (expit(Ai @ w_i) - yi)) / len(yi)
    if k in log_ks:
        path_i.append((k, w_i.copy()))
    if k in checkpoints:
        cos = w_i @ w_hat / (np.linalg.norm(w_i) * np.linalg.norm(w_hat))
        rows.append({"k": k, "||w_k||": np.linalg.norm(w_i), "angle to w_hat (degrees)": np.degrees(np.arccos(min(1.0, cos))),
                     "geometric margin": (si * (Ai @ w_i)).min() / np.linalg.norm(w_i),
                     "training loss": np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, -si * (Ai @ w_i)))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4g}"))
norms = [r["||w_k||"] for r in rows]
print(f"increase of ||w_k|| per decade of k: {np.round(np.diff(norms), 2)}; the theorem predicts ||w_hat|| ln(10) = {np.linalg.norm(w_hat) * np.log(10):.2f}")





# Figure 7.11 — gradient descent on separable data: the decision boundary and the growth of the weights
def figure_7_11():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.0))
    ax = axes[0]
    for cls, color, marker, label in [(0, BLUE, "o", "setosa"), (1, ORANGE, "s", "versicolor")]:
        ax.plot(Zi[yi == cls, 0], Zi[yi == cls, 1], marker, color=color, ms=4.5, mec="white", mew=0.5, ls="", label=label)
    x1 = np.linspace(Zi[:, 0].min() - 0.2, Zi[:, 0].max() + 0.2, 100)
    ax.plot(x1, -(w_hat[0] + w_hat[1] * x1) / w_hat[2], color="k", lw=2.2, label="maximum margin")
    for (k, wk), color in zip([p for p in path_i if p[0] in (10, 1000, 1_000_000)], [SKY, GREEN, VERMILION]):
        ax.plot(x1, -(wk[0] + wk[1] * x1) / wk[2], color=color, lw=1.6, ls="--", label=f"GD after $k = 10^{int(round(np.log10(k)))}$")
    ax.set(xlim=(x1.min(), x1.max()), ylim=(Zi[:, 1].min() - 0.3, Zi[:, 1].max() + 0.3),
           xlabel="standardized petal length", ylabel="standardized petal width", title="(a) the boundary after $k$ steps")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.17), ncol=3)
    ax = axes[1]
    kk = np.array([p[0] for p in path_i])
    nn = np.array([np.linalg.norm(p[1]) for p in path_i])
    ax.plot(kk, nn, color=BLUE, lw=2, label=r"$\|\mathbf{w}_k\|$ (measured)")
    ref = np.linalg.norm(w_hat) * np.log(kk / 1000) + nn[list(kk).index(1000)]
    ax.plot(kk, ref, color=VERMILION, lw=1.5, ls="--", label=r"$\|\hat{\mathbf{w}}\|\,\ln k$, anchored at $k = 10^3$")
    ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="iteration $k$", ylabel=r"norm of the weights", title="(b) the weights grow like $\\ln k$")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="upper left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_11()



The hard-margin solution has two active constraints (two support vectors), a geometric margin of 0.646 and a norm of 1.549. After 

103 steps the gradient-descent direction is within 2.1^\circ of it and its margin is 96\% of the maximum; after 

106 steps the margin is 99\% of the maximum (0.640 against 0.646). The norm of the weights grows like the theorem says: by about 2.8, 3.1 and 3.3 per decade of iterations, approaching \|\hat{\mathbf{w}}\|\ln 10 = 3.57, while the training loss falls from 3.5 \cdot 10^{-2} to 

10-6: the loss is already below 

10-3 after a thousand steps, but the iterates keep moving, slowly, toward the max-margin direction. One detail deserves honesty: the angle is not monotone, it falls to 2.1^\circ at k = 10^3 and then rises slowly to 3.0^\circ at k = 10^6. The theorem guarantees convergence of the direction, with a correction \boldsymbol\rho_k that is bounded only when the support vectors span the data, and here two support vectors cannot span the three-dimensional augmented space; this is consistent with a slowly growing correction, but we have not tested that explanation. The practical message is the one of the theorem: the direction converges extremely slowly (as 1/\ln k), and nobody runs gradient descent long enough to reach it exactly, but the region in which early-stopped solutions lie is close to the support vector machine, and, in this experiment, very close after a thousand steps.

Chapter 7 — Optimization: Gradient Descent and Stochastic Gradient Descent

records.content:
Different coordinates of a model can have gradients of very different sizes (the raw Diabetes problem is an example), and in sparse problems some coordinates are updated rarely. Adaptive methods give each coordinate its own step size, built from the history of its gradients. All use the elementwise square \mathbf{g}^2 of the gradient.

AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan and Singer, 2011) accumulates \mathbf{G}_k = \mathbf{G}_{k-1} + \mathbf{g}_k^2 and moves by -\eta\,\mathbf{g}_k/(\sqrt{\mathbf{G}_k} + \varepsilon): coordinates with large past gradients get small steps.

RMSprop (Hinton, 2012) replaces the sum by a moving average, \mathbf{v}_k = \rho\mathbf{v}_{k-1} + (1 - \rho)\mathbf{g}_k^2, so that the memory is finite and the steps do not shrink to zero.

Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) adds momentum and a correction for the zero initialization of the averages:
\mathbf{m}_k = \beta_1\mathbf{m}_{k-1} + (1 - \beta_1)\mathbf{g}_k, \quad
\mathbf{v}_k = \beta_2\mathbf{v}_{k-1} + (1 - \beta_2)\mathbf{g}_k^2, \quad
\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\,\frac{\mathbf{m}_k/(1 - \beta_1^k)}{\sqrt{\mathbf{v}_k/(1 - \beta_2^k)} + \varepsilon},


with the usual defaults \beta_1 = 0.9, \beta_2 = 0.999, \varepsilon = 10^{-8}.

In the language of Section 7.4, these methods build a diagonal preconditioner from the gradient history, adapted at run time instead of fixed by the units of the features. Their step size is no longer in units of 1/L: the coordinate-wise move has size of order \eta whatever the scale of the gradient, which is why \eta for Adam is typically between 

10-4 and 

10-1 in the units of the parameters.

The next experiment is a comparison on a deterministic problem, with full gradients, so that only the update rule matters: Diabetes least squares in raw units (where the diagonal rescaling matters most) and standardized. For AdaGrad and Adam the step size \eta is chosen from a logarithmic grid by the final suboptimality after 3{,}000 iterations, that is with hindsight, which is favorable to them; gradient descent uses \eta = 1/L. The numbers describe this problem and this tuning protocol, not a general ranking.

def adaptive_run(grad, record, w0, kind, eta, iters, eps=1e-8, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999):
    w = w0.copy()
    m, v, out = np.zeros_like(w), np.zeros_like(w), np.empty(iters)
    for k in range(1, iters + 1):
        out[k - 1] = record(w)
        g = grad(w)
        if kind == "adagrad":
            v += g**2
            w = w - eta * g / (np.sqrt(v) + eps)
        else:                                                    # Adam
            m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g
            v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * g**2
            w = w - eta * (m / (1 - beta1**k)) / (np.sqrt(v / (1 - beta2**k)) + eps)
    return out


ITERS_A = 3000
problems = {"raw units": (H_raw, b_raw), "standardized": (H_d, b_d)}
curves_a, rows = {}, []
for pname, (H, b) in problems.items():
    ws = np.linalg.solve(H, b)
    grad_q = lambda w, H=H, b=b: H @ w - b
    rec_q = lambda w, H=H, ws=ws: 0.5 * (w - ws) @ H @ (w - ws)
    L_q = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)[-1]
    runs = {"gradient descent": (1 / L_q, momentum_run(grad_q, rec_q, np.zeros(10), 1 / L_q, lambda k: 0.0, ITERS_A, "hb"))}
    for kind, eta_grid in [("adagrad", [0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10]), ("adam", [0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10])]:
        cands = []
        for eta in eta_grid:
            c = adaptive_run(grad_q, rec_q, np.zeros(10), kind, eta, ITERS_A)
            if np.isfinite(c[-1]):
                cands.append((c[-1], eta, c))
        _, eta_best, c_best = min(cands, key=lambda t: t[0])
        runs["AdaGrad" if kind == "adagrad" else "Adam"] = (eta_best, c_best)
    curves_a[pname] = runs
    for name, (eta, c) in runs.items():
        rows.append({"problem": pname, "method": name, "eta": eta, **{f"gap, k = {k}": max(c[k - 1], 0.0) for k in (10, 100, 1000, 3000)}})
print(f"initial suboptimality: raw {curves_a['raw units']['gradient descent'][1][0]:.0f}, "
      f"standardized {curves_a['standardized']['gradient descent'][1][0]:.0f}")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))
c_adam = curves_a["raw units"]["Adam"][1]
print(f"Adam on raw units: smallest value {c_adam.min():.1e}, then the largest suboptimality between k = 1200 and 3000 is {c_adam[1199:].max():.1e}")



# Figure 7.12 — adaptive methods on the Diabetes least-squares problem
def figure_7_12():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.0), sharey=True)
    for ax, pname in zip(axes, problems):
        for (name, (eta, c)), color in zip(curves_a[pname].items(), [BLUE, ORANGE, VERMILION]):
            ax.plot(np.arange(1, ITERS_A + 1), np.maximum(c, 1e-12), color=color, lw=1.8, label=name)
        ax.set(yscale="log", xscale="log", xlabel="iteration $k$", title=f"({'a' if pname == 'raw units' else 'b'}) {pname}")
    axes[0].set_ylabel(r"suboptimality $f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\ast$")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="lower left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_12()



On raw units, gradient descent has removed only 94\% of the initial suboptimality (1569 \to 86) after 3{,}000 iterations, while AdaGrad reaches 0.15 and Adam 

10-14 (machine precision): the per-coordinate scaling does for the units what the standardization of Section 7.4 does by hand, since the diagonal rescaling brings \kappa from 7.4 \cdot 10^4 to 418. On the standardized problem there is nothing left for a diagonal rescaling to fix, and gradient descent and AdaGrad are close (8.7 \cdot 10^{-6} against 4.8 \cdot 10^{-7} at k = 3000); Adam is much faster at k = 1000 (8.5 \cdot 10^{-4} against 0.13), but note that it contains momentum, and the heavy ball of Section 7.5 is also far faster than gradient descent on this problem. Two warnings are visible in the table. Adam’s first iterations overshoot: its suboptimality after ten iterations is 6{,}750 on the raw problem, four times the initial value, because each coordinate moves by about \eta per step whatever the size of its gradient. On the raw problem there is a second symptom: after Adam has reached machine precision (a suboptimality of 4 \cdot 10^{-28} at its best), the suboptimality jumps back up in isolated spikes, the largest of about 3 \cdot 10^{3} between k = 1200 and k = 3000, because the second-moment average of a gradient that has become tiny decays and the normalized step \eta\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v} stops being small; the spikes are visible in Figure 7.12. And we tuned \eta with hindsight for both adaptive methods. In the stochastic setting, where Adam is mostly used, there is no equivalent of the contraction of Theorem 7.3; Adam can fail to converge even on convex problems with a constant \beta_2 (Reddi, Kale and Kumar, 2018), and in practice it is run with a decaying step and a short warm-up. The rule of thumb that survives is modest: adaptive methods are less sensitive to the scale of the features and of the gradients, they are not a substitute for standardizing the inputs, and they do not remove the need to tune \eta.

records.content:
Everything above rested on convexity: every critical point of a convex function is a global minimizer, and gradient descent finds it. The models of the next chapters are convex (support vector machines, Chapter 8, and the lasso of Chapter 10), but the neural networks of Part IV are not, and it is worth seeing now, on two small functions, what changes. Both functions are constructed, not data.

At a critical point \nabla f(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0} the eigenvalues of the Hessian tell what kind of point it is: all positive, a local minimum; all negative, a local maximum; some positive and some negative, a saddle point. Gradient descent is attracted to minima and repelled by maxima, but a saddle is attractive along the directions of positive curvature and repulsive along those of negative curvature, so the iteration approaches it and then, unless it is exactly on the attractive manifold, leaves along the repulsive direction. The test case is f(x, y) = \frac{x^4}4 - \frac{x^2}2 + \frac{y^2}2, with a saddle at the origin (Hessian \mathrm{diag}(-1, 1)) and two minima at (\pm 1, 0) (Hessian \mathrm{diag}(2, 1)). Near the origin the x-coordinate evolves as x_{k+1} = x_k(1 + \eta - \eta x_k^2) \approx (1 + \eta)x_k: it grows geometrically at rate 1 + \eta\lvert\lambda_{\min}\rvert, so starting at distance \lvert x_0\rvert from the saddle the escape takes about \ln(1/\lvert x_0\rvert)/\ln(1 + \eta) iterations, plus the time needed to cross the nonlinear region. If x_0 is exactly zero, however, the iteration stays on the line x = 0 and converges to the saddle.

eta_s = 0.1
rows = []
for x0 in [1e-2, 1e-6, 1e-12, 0.0]:
    p = np.array([x0, 1.0])
    hit = None
    for k in range(1, 5001):
        p = p - eta_s * np.array([p[0] ** 3 - p[0], p[1]])        # gradient of x^4/4 - x^2/2 + y^2/2
        if abs(abs(p[0]) - 1) < 1e-3:
            hit = k
            break
    est = np.log(1 / x0) / np.log(1 + eta_s) if x0 > 0 else np.inf
    rows.append({"x0": x0, "iterations to reach a minimum": hit if hit else "never (5000 run)",
                 "linearized estimate": est, "difference": (hit - est) if hit else np.nan})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3g}"))
print(f"at the exact saddle start, the final point after 5000 steps is {p.round(6)}")



The measured escape times, 77, 173 and 318 iterations, exceed the linearized estimates by almost the same amount (28 to 29 iterations), the time of the nonlinear crossing, which does not depend on x_0. A starting point that is 

10-12 away from the saddle needs only four times as many steps as one that is 

10-2 away: a saddle is not a trap for gradient descent, except for the single starting point that sits exactly on its stable manifold. This is a general fact (“gradient descent almost surely avoids strict saddle points”, Lee et al., 2016), and in SGD the noise of the gradient moves the iterate off the stable manifold by itself, which is one of the reasons why SGD works better than the theory of Section 7.6 would lead one to expect on non-convex problems.

The second difficulty is that there may be several local minima, and which one gradient descent finds depends on where it starts. The Himmelblau function f(x, y) = (x^2 + y - 11)^2 + (x + y^2 - 7)^2, a classical test function, has four minima, all with f = 0. We start gradient descent from every point of a 201 \times 201 grid on [-5, 5]^2 and record the minimum it reaches.

def himmelblau_grad(P):
    x, y = P[..., 0], P[..., 1]
    return np.stack([4 * x * (x**2 + y - 11) + 2 * (x + y**2 - 7), 2 * (x**2 + y - 11) + 4 * y * (x + y**2 - 7)], axis=-1)


minima = np.array([[3.0, 2.0], [-2.805118, 3.131312], [-3.779310, -3.283186], [3.584428, -1.848126]])
print("largest gradient component at the four known minima:", np.abs(himmelblau_grad(minima)).max().round(5))
gx = np.linspace(-5, 5, 201)
P0 = np.stack(np.meshgrid(gx, gx), axis=-1).reshape(-1, 2)
P = P0.copy()
for _ in range(3000):
    P = P - 0.005 * himmelblau_grad(P)
dist = np.linalg.norm(P[:, None, :] - minima[None], axis=2)
basin = dist.argmin(axis=1)
converged = dist.min(axis=1) < 1e-2
print(f"starting points that converge to a minimum: {converged.mean():.3f}")
print("share of the starting points that reach each minimum:", np.round([(basin[converged] == i).mean() for i in range(4)], 3))





# Figure 7.13 — a saddle point and four basins of attraction (constructed functions)
def figure_7_13():
    from matplotlib.colors import ListedColormap
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.2))
    ax = axes[0]
    g1, g2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-1.7, 1.7, 300), np.linspace(-1.3, 1.3, 300))
    ax.contour(g1, g2, g1**4 / 4 - g1**2 / 2 + g2**2 / 2, levels=np.linspace(-0.2, 1.4, 12), colors="0.7", linewidths=0.8)
    for x0, color, lab in [(0.01, BLUE, r"$x_0 = +10^{-2}$"), (-0.01, ORANGE, r"$x_0 = -10^{-2}$"), (0.0, VERMILION, r"$x_0 = 0$ (exactly)")]:
        p = np.array([x0, 1.0])
        path = [p]
        for _ in range(160):
            p = p - eta_s * np.array([p[0] ** 3 - p[0], p[1]])
            path.append(p)
        path = np.array(path)
        ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], "-", color=color, lw=1.8, label=lab)
        ax.plot(*path[0], "o", color=color, ms=5, mec="white")
    ax.plot([0], [0], "x", color="k", ms=9, mew=2)
    ax.plot([-1, 1], [0, 0], "*", color="k", ms=11)
    ax.set(xlabel="$x$", ylabel="$y$", title="(a) the saddle at the origin ($\\times$), two minima ($\\star$)")
    ax.legend(frameon=True, framealpha=0.9, edgecolor="none", fontsize=8, loc="lower center", ncol=1)
    ax = axes[1]
    cmap = ListedColormap([BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN, PURPLE])
    ax.imshow(basin.reshape(201, 201), origin="lower", extent=(-5, 5, -5, 5), cmap=cmap, alpha=0.55, interpolation="nearest")
    G1, G2 = np.meshgrid(gx, gx)
    ax.contour(G1, G2, (G1**2 + G2 - 11) ** 2 + (G1 + G2**2 - 7) ** 2, levels=[5, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400], colors="0.35", linewidths=0.6)
    ax.plot(minima[:, 0], minima[:, 1], "*", color="k", ms=12, mec="white")
    ax.set(xlabel="$x_0$", ylabel="$y_0$", title="(b) which minimum gradient descent reaches")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_7_13()



The four basins, each reached from about a quarter of the starting points (25.6\%, 26.0\%, 23.7\% and 24.7\%), are interleaved, with boundaries that wind around the saddles between the minima: a small change of the starting point can change the answer. For this function the four minima are equally good (f = 0), but in general they are not, and the quality of the solution then depends on the initialization and on the path: this is the reason why the random seed matters for neural networks, and why the chapters on deep networks (Chapters 14 and 15) pay so much attention to initialization.

We close the chapter by putting side by side what the experiments measured. The first table reports, for the logistic regression of Section 7.3.4 (426 examples, 31 parameters, local condition number 24), the number of evaluations of the gradient needed to bring the suboptimality below 

10-8. It is a cost in gradients (each is a pass over the data, of the order of n p operations); Newton’s method needs 7 steps, each of which also forms and solves with the Hessian.

cost_rows = [
    ("gradient descent, eta = 1/L_glob = 0.30", iterations_to(gd_runs["1/L_glob = 0.30"]), "no tuning, safe by the theory"),
    ("gradient descent, eta = 8.7 (largest stable constant step)", iterations_to(gd_runs["8.7"]), "needs the unknown local L"),
    ("gradient descent with backtracking", len(gaps_bt) - 1, f"plus {n_func_bt - len(gaps_bt)} extra function evaluations"),
    ("Nesterov (strongly convex version)", iterations_to(curves_b["Nesterov, strongly convex version"]), "needs mu and L"),
    ("heavy ball, beta = 0.9", iterations_to(curves_b["heavy ball, beta = 0.9"]), "beta tuned by hand"),
    ("L-BFGS", int(hist[k_lb, 1]), "memory of a few gradient pairs"),
    ("Newton", 7, "7 Hessians and 7 linear solves"),
]
print(pd.DataFrame(cost_rows, columns=["method", "gradient evaluations to gap < 1e-8", "remark"]).to_string(index=False))
print(f"SGD, batch size 1, best constant step of the grid: suboptimality after {EPOCHS} epochs "
      f"(= {EPOCHS} gradient-equivalents): {runs_sgd['constant eta = 0.03'][-1]:.1e}")



The same ordering is not universal: it depends on n, on the number of parameters p, on the conditioning and on the accuracy required. The guide below summarizes what the theory of this chapter and the experiments suggest.

Four rules of practice follow from the chapter. (1) Standardize the inputs before anything else (Section 7.4): it is the cheapest way to gain two or more orders of magnitude. (2) Regularization helps the optimization as well as the statistics: it adds \lambda to the smallest curvature (Section 7.2.2). (3) For a smooth convex problem of moderate size, use a library solver (L-BFGS or Newton), which chooses its own step by line search; for large n, use SGD with mini-batches, a decaying step size tuned on a logarithmic grid, and monitor the training objective. (4) An iterative solver that stops at a fixed number of epochs is a regularized estimator: treat the number of iterations as a hyperparameter, to be chosen on validation data (Chapter 5), together with the other ones.

records.content:
Gradient and steepest descent. The gradients of the least-squares, logistic and softmax losses all have the form (features) \times (residual) and are checked by finite differences (relative error 

10-8 to 

10-10). The negative gradient is the steepest descent direction (Cauchy–Schwarz); gradient descent is \mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k).

Curvature. L-smoothness (\nabla^2 f \preceq L\mathbf{I}) and \mu-strong convexity (\nabla^2 f \succeq \mu\mathbf{I}) define the condition number \kappa = L/\mu. For least squares the eigenvalues of the Hessian are \sigma_j^2/n + \lambda, the singular values of Chapter 6. On Diabetes, \kappa = 7.4 \cdot 10^4 in raw units, 418 standardized, 37 with \lambda = 0.1 and 4.9 with \lambda = 1.

GD on a quadratic (Theorem 7.3). The error along the j-th eigenvector is multiplied by (1 - \eta\lambda_j) per step: convergence iff \eta < 2/L, best step 2/(L + \mu) with rate (\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1), at most \kappa\ln(1/\varepsilon) iterations for \eta = 1/L. On Diabetes: 5{,}677 iterations for \eta = 1/L (predicted at most 5{,}766), 2{,}856 for the best step (2{,}886), divergence for 2.1/L.

Convex and strongly convex functions. The descent lemma gives f(\mathbf{w}_k) - f^\ast \le \lVert\mathbf{w}_0 - \mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2/(2\eta k) (Theorem 7.4) and, with strong convexity, the contraction \rho = \max\{\lvert 1 - \eta\mu\rvert, \lvert 1 - \eta L\rvert\} (Theorem 7.5). For the logistic regression on Breast Cancer the global bound L = 3.30 is 14 times the curvature at the minimizer (0.23): 1/L needs 1{,}631 iterations, \eta = 8 needs 69, and the threshold of stability is 2/L_{\text{loc}} = 8.7 (above it the iteration ends in a cycle). The O(1/k) bound holds and is loose by orders of magnitude.

Choosing the step. Backtracking with the Armijo condition terminates for every L-smooth function (Proposition 7.6): 57 steps and 169 function evaluations here. L-BFGS needs 19 iterations and Newton’s method 7, at a higher cost per step.

Conditioning. Rescaling the variables is preconditioning (Proposition 7.7): standardization is the Jacobi preconditioner and Newton’s method the ideal one. On Diabetes it reduces the iterations needed for a thousandfold reduction of the distance from 509{,}391 to 2{,}799; a ridge penalty of 0.1 reduces them to 176.

Momentum. The heavy ball has rate (\sqrt\kappa - 1)/(\sqrt\kappa + 1) on quadratics (Theorem 7.8) and Nesterov’s method O(1/k^2) on every smooth convex function (Theorem 7.9, optimal). On Diabetes, 190 iterations against 2{,}856 for the best gradient descent; on the logistic regression, 146 against 1{,}631. Momentum methods are not descent methods.

SGD. The mini-batch gradient is unbiased with variance \sigma^2/B, and the variance does not vanish at the minimizer (0.27 per example on Breast Cancer, against 5.8 at the start). A constant step gives a noise floor of order L\eta\sigma^2/(2\mu) (Theorem 7.11): on Breast Cancer 8.3 \cdot 10^{-2}, 8.6 \cdot 10^{-3}, 5.3 \cdot 10^{-4} for \eta = 0.3, 0.1, 0.03. A decreasing step \eta_k = \beta/(\gamma + k) converges as O(1/k) (Theorem 7.12): 3.4 \cdot 10^{-5} after 300 epochs. Averaging the iterates lowered a floor sixfold but did not remove it. The floor is ordered like \eta/B (linear scaling rule). On this small problem full-batch GD (69 epochs to 

10-8) is far better than SGD.

SGD in practice. On Digits the best step grows with the batch size (0.1/L, 1/L, 10/L, 30/L for B = 1, 16, 128, 1347); after 30 epochs the suboptimality is 0.0149 for full-batch GD against 0.0018 to 0.0044 for SGD, with test accuracies 0.956 against 0.969 to 0.971 (exact minimizer: 0.973).

Early stopping is implicit ridge. GD from zero multiplies the least-squares coefficient along the j-th eigenvector by 1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^k, ridge by h_j/(h_j + \lambda), and with \lambda = 1/(\eta k) the first is between one and two times the second (Proposition 7.13; both bounds attained). On Diabetes the test MSE falls from 2848 to 2814 at k = 7; in raw units the path is monotone and never beats least squares: early stopping regularizes in the geometry of the parametrization.

Implicit bias. On separable data GD on the unpenalized logistic loss diverges in norm like \ln k and its direction converges, at rate O(1/\ln k), to the maximum-margin direction (Theorem 7.14). On Iris the margin is at 96\% of the maximum after 

103 steps and at 99\% after 

104, the norm grows by 3.3 per decade at the end (theory: 3.57) and the angle is not monotone. On Breast Cancer (31 parameters) the direction converges far more slowly (angle 9^\circ after 

106 steps) and the early-stopped iterates classify better than the limit (Exercise 7.10).

Adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam) build a diagonal preconditioner from the gradient history. On raw Diabetes, GD still has a suboptimality of 86 after 3,000 iterations while Adam reaches machine precision; they are less sensitive to the scale of the inputs, not a substitute for standardizing them, and their constant-step behavior has overshoots and instabilities.

Non-convex functions. Saddle points repel gradient descent except from a measure-zero set: escape takes \ln(1/\lvert x_0\rvert)/\ln(1 + \eta) plus a constant (\approx 28) iterations. With several minima the result depends on the initialization (four basins of about 25\% each for Himmelblau’s function).

Exercise 7.1 ★ — Gradient descent by hand. Let f(\mathbf{w}) = w_1^2 + 4w_2^2 and \mathbf{w}_0 = (4, 1). (a) Compute the Hessian, L, \mu, \kappa and the minimizer. (b) Run three steps of gradient descent with \eta = 1/L and write the general iterate. (c) What is the best constant step size, what is the rate, and what are the first three iterates with that step? (d) For which values of \eta does the iteration converge? Describe what happens for \eta = 1/4.

Hint. The Hessian is diagonal, so each coordinate is an independent one-dimensional problem: w_{j,k+1} = (1 - \eta\lambda_j)w_{j,k} (Theorem 7.3).

Exercise 7.2 ★★ — The smoothness constant of a logistic regression. (a) Show that \ell(m) = \log(1 + e^{-m}) satisfies 0 < \ell''(m) \le \frac14 and deduce that the mean logistic loss with penalty \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 is L-smooth with L = \frac{1}{4n}\lVert\mathbf{X}\rVert_2^2 + \lambda. (b) For the data of Exercise 6.3(a), x = (-1, 0, 1) and y = (0, 1, 1), with an intercept and \lambda = 0, compute L, and show that at (b, w) = (0, 0) the Hessian has largest eigenvalue exactly L (the bound is tight at the origin). (c) Take one step of gradient descent with \eta = 1/L from (0, 0), compute the new point and the values of f, and verify the inequality of the descent lemma (Proposition 7.2).

Hint. (a) \ell'' = \sigma(m)\sigma(-m), and \sigma(m)\sigma(-m) = \frac14\operatorname{sech}^2(m/2) or, simply, s(1 - s) \le \frac14 for s \in (0, 1). The Hessian is \frac1n\mathbf{X}^\top\mathrm{diag}(s_i(1 - s_i))\mathbf{X}. (b) \tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top\tilde{\mathbf{X}} = \mathrm{diag}(3, 2). (c) The gradient at the origin is \frac1n\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top(\tfrac12\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{y}).

Exercise 7.3 ★★ — The heavy ball on a quadratic. Let f be a quadratic with eigenvalues between \mu = 1 and L = 100. (a) What are the best step size of gradient descent, its rate, and the number of iterations needed to reduce the error by 

10-6 (solve \rho^k = 10^{-6})? (b) Compute the heavy-ball parameters \eta and \beta of Theorem 7.8, the rate, and the number of iterations from \rho^k = 10^{-6}. (c) For the eigenvalues \lambda = \mu and \lambda = L, write the characteristic polynomial z^2 - (1 + \beta - \eta\lambda)z + \beta and verify that it has a double root, of modulus \sqrt\beta.

Hint. \kappa = 100, \sqrt\kappa = 10. In (c), a quadratic has a double root when its discriminant vanishes.

Exercise 7.4 ★★★ — SGD for a mean. Let x_0, x_1, \dots be independent with mean m and variance \sigma^2 and consider the one-dimensional problem f(w) = \frac12\mathbb{E}(w - x)^2, with the stochastic gradient g_k = w_k - x_k (so L = \mu = 1 and \mathbb{E}\lVert g - \nabla f\rVert^2 = \sigma^2). (a) With \eta_k = 1/(k + 1), show that w_k is the sample mean of x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}, so that \mathbb{E}\,f(w_k) - f^\ast = \sigma^2/(2k), and compare with Theorem 7.12 (this step is the limiting case \beta = 1/\mu, \gamma = 1 of its hypothesis \beta > 1/\mu). (b) With a constant step \eta \in (0, 1], show that \operatorname{Var}(w_k) converges to \eta\sigma^2/(2 - \eta), and compare \mathbb{E}f - f^\ast = \frac12\operatorname{Var} with the floor L\eta\sigma^2/(2\mu) of Theorem 7.11. (c) Compute both quantities for \eta = 0.1 and \sigma^2 = 1.

Hint. The recursion is w_{k+1} - m = (1 - \eta_k)(w_k - m) + \eta_k(x_k - m). For (a), \eta_0 = 1 gives w_1 = x_0 and then w_{k+1} = \frac{k}{k + 1}w_k + \frac1{k + 1}x_k. For (b), the variance satisfies V_{k+1} = (1 - \eta)^2V_k + \eta^2\sigma^2, whose fixed point is \eta^2\sigma^2/(1 - (1 - \eta)^2).

Exercise 7.5 ★★ — Early stopping and ridge in two directions. The Hessian of a least-squares problem is \mathbf{H} = \mathrm{diag}(1, 0.01), and gradient descent with \eta = 1 starts from \mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}. (a) Write the filter factors \varphi_j(k) = 1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^k of the two directions. (b) Compute the factor of the second direction for k = 1, 10, 100, 1000 and compare it with the ridge factor h_2/(h_2 + \lambda) with \lambda = 1/(\eta k). (c) What is the smallest k for which the second direction is at least half recovered? Which ridge penalty gives the factor \frac12 exactly? (d) Verify that each ratio of (b) lies in [1, 2] (Proposition 7.13).

Hint. For the first direction \eta h_1 = 1, so \varphi_1(k) = 1 for every k \ge 1. In (c) solve 0.99^k \le \frac12. The ridge factor is \frac12 when \lambda = h_2.

records.content: We now have the machinery to compute the models of the book, and a precise understanding of what the computation does: its speed is governed by the conditioning of the problem, its noise by the batch size and the step, and stopping early is a form of regularization. Chapter 8 studies the support vector machine, obtained by replacing the logistic loss \log(1 + e^{-m}) by the hinge loss \max(0, 1 - m). The hinge loss is not differentiable at m = 1, so Theorem 7.3 and its relatives do not apply directly: the next chapter will need subgradients or the dual problem, and will show that the solution depends only on the examples near the boundary, those that Section 7.7.3 called support vectors, for which the margin bound of Section 3.8.4 is the natural guarantee. Chapter 9 exploits the dual form of ridge regression (Proposition 6.12) to obtain kernels. Chapter 10 replaces the \ell_2 penalty by the \ell_1 penalty, which sets coefficients exactly to zero and performs feature selection, and which is again non-differentiable, so that plain gradient descent will not be enough. Chapter 11 returns to nonlinear models with decision trees and ensembles. In Part IV, Chapters 14 and 15 build neural networks and backpropagation, which is nothing but the computation of the gradient of Section 7.2.1 for a composition of functions; the optimizers of this chapter, SGD with momentum and Adam above all, are then used on non-convex losses, with the learning-rate recipes of Section 7.7.1.

Chapter 7 ended with a curious fact: gradient descent on the logistic loss, run on separable data, drifts toward the separating hyperplane with the largest margin, and that hyperplane depends only on the few training examples that sit on the margin. This chapter starts from that hyperplane. We derive the support vector machine from the geometry of the margin, obtain its dual problem and see why the solution is sparse in the examples, extend it to data that cannot be separated with the hinge loss, solve it with a subgradient method and with the SMO algorithm, and measure what the margin buys in generalization.

A linear classifier predicts \operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b). The hyperplane H = \{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = 0\} separates the space in two half-spaces, and the size of the score of a point says how far from H it is.

Proposition 8.1 (distance to a hyperplane)

The distance from a point \mathbf{x} to the hyperplane H is \lvert\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\rvert/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert. Consequently, if y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\ge 1 for all i and equality holds for at least one example of each class, the two parallel hyperplanes \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = \pm 1 are at distance 2/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert from each other, and no training point lies between them.

Proof

Let \mathbf{x}_0 \in H be the point of H closest to \mathbf{x}. The vector \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0 is orthogonal to H, hence parallel to \mathbf{w}: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_0 + t\,\mathbf{w}/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert for a real t, whose absolute value is the distance. Then \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_0 + b + t\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = t\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert, so \lvert t\rvert = \lvert\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\rvert/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert. A point on \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = 1 is at distance 1/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert from H, and one on \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = -1 at the same distance on the other side. \square

Suppose the training set is linearly separable: some (\mathbf{w}, b) has y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) > 0 for all i. There are then infinitely many separating hyperplanes (Figure 8.1), all with zero training error, and the question is which one to choose. The geometric margin of (\mathbf{w}, b) is the distance from H to the closest training point, \gamma = \min_i y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert. The score does not change in sign if we multiply (\mathbf{w}, b) by a positive constant, and the margin is invariant under that change, so we may fix the scale by requiring that the closest points have score exactly \pm 1. In this scale \gamma = 1/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert (Proposition 8.1) and maximizing the margin is the same as minimizing \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert:\boxed{\ \min_{\mathbf{w}, b}\ \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 \quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\ \ge\ 1,\quad i = 1, \dots, n.\ }
\tag{hard-margin primal}

This is a convex quadratic program: a strictly convex objective in \mathbf{w} with n linear inequality constraints. It has a solution if and only if the data are separable, and then the solution \hat{\mathbf{w}} is unique (the objective is strictly convex in \mathbf{w} and the feasible set is convex). The reason for choosing this hyperplane is the margin bound of Theorem 3.7: with the constraints y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)\ge 1 the first term of the bound (the fraction of points with margin below \gamma = 1) is zero, and the second term is proportional to \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert, which is the quantity that the SVM minimizes. Among all the separating hyperplanes, it is the one with the smallest value of the bound.

The next two cells set up the data of this section. The first is Worked example 8.1, five points in the plane small enough to solve by hand. The second is the data of Figure 8.1(b): the petal length and width of the setosa and versicolor flowers of Iris (100 flowers, 50 in each class), a real separable problem in two dimensions.

Take the negative points \mathbf{x}_1 = (0, 0), \mathbf{x}_2 = (2, 0) and the positive points \mathbf{x}_3 = (1, 2), \mathbf{x}_4 = (3, 3), \mathbf{x}_5 = (0, 4). This data set is constructed, to be solved in closed form. Looking at the picture (Figure 8.1(a)), the closest points of the two classes are \mathbf{x}_3 and the segment between \mathbf{x}_1 and \mathbf{x}_2: guess that the support vectors are \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_3, that is, that the constraints of these three points hold with equality and the others are slack. The equalities are\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{x}_1:&\quad -(b) = 1 &&\Rightarrow\ b = -1,\\
\mathbf{x}_2:&\quad -(2w_1 + b) = 1 &&\Rightarrow\ 2w_1 = -b - 1 = 0,\ \ w_1 = 0,\\
\mathbf{x}_3:&\quad w_1 + 2w_2 + b = 1 &&\Rightarrow\ 2w_2 = 2,\ \ w_2 = 1.
\end{aligned}

So \mathbf{w} = (0, 1), b = -1, and the margin is 1/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 1 (the two margin hyperplanes, w_2 = 0 and w_2 = 2, are at distance 2). The guess is right if the other constraints hold: \mathbf{x}_4 has score 3 - 1 = 2 \ge 1 and \mathbf{x}_5 has 4 - 1 = 3 \ge 1. That the guess is the optimal solution is what the dual of the next section proves: there we shall find \boldsymbol\alpha = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac12, 0, 0). The code below solves the problem numerically (scikit-learn’s SVC with a very large C is a hard-margin SVM when the data are separable) and also with a general-purpose optimizer applied directly to the primal.

X_we = np.array([[0, 0], [2, 0], [1, 2], [3, 3], [0, 4]], dtype=float)           # constructed example
y_we = np.array([-1, -1, 1, 1, 1], dtype=float)

hard_we = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-10).fit(X_we, y_we)
print("sklearn:      w =", hard_we.coef_.round(6).ravel(), " b =", hard_we.intercept_.round(6), " support vectors:", hard_we.support_ + 1)
print("alpha_i y_i for the support vectors:", hard_we.dual_coef_.round(6).ravel())

constraints = [{"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda v, i=i: y_we[i] * (X_we[i] @ v[:2] + v[2]) - 1} for i in range(len(y_we))]
primal = minimize(lambda v: 0.5 * v[:2] @ v[:2], x0=np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.1]), constraints=constraints, method="SLSQP",
                  options={"ftol": 1e-14, "maxiter": 500})
print("direct primal: w =", primal.x[:2].round(6), " b =", primal.x[2].round(6))
print("scores of the five points:", (X_we @ hard_we.coef_.ravel() + hard_we.intercept_).round(4))

8.2.2 The dual problem and the support vectors

records.content:
The primal has d + 1 unknowns and n constraints. Attaching a multiplier \alpha_i \ge 0 to each constraint gives the Lagrangian\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol\alpha) = \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 - \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i\big[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) - 1\big],

and the derivation below shows how it leads to a different problem, in the n unknowns \alpha_i, whose solution gives the one of the primal.

Theorem 8.2 (dual problem and KKT conditions of the hard-margin SVM)

Let the data be separable. The primal has a unique solution \hat{\mathbf{w}}, and there are multipliers \hat\alpha_i \ge 0 that solve the dual problem\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\ \ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_i\alpha_j\,y_iy_j\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j
\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \alpha_i\ge 0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iy_i = 0,

with no gap between the primal and the dual optimal values. The solutions are linked by\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_{i=1}^n\hat\alpha_i\,y_i\,\mathbf{x}_i,
\qquad
\hat\alpha_i\,\big[y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b) - 1\big] = 0\ \text{ for every } i\quad\text{(complementary slackness)}.

Consequently: (i) only the examples on the margin (y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b) = 1), the support vectors, can have \hat\alpha_i > 0, and \hat{\mathbf{w}} is a combination of them alone; (ii) \lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\hat\alpha_i, so the margin is 1/\sqrt{\sum_i\hat\alpha_i}; (iii) the data enter the dual only through the inner products \mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j; (iv) the prediction is \operatorname{sign}\big(\sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x} + \hat b\big), and the intercept is obtained from any support vector, \hat b = y_k - \hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_k.

Proof

The dual function. For fixed \boldsymbol\alpha \ge 0, minimize \mathcal{L} over (\mathbf{w}, b). The Lagrangian is convex and differentiable in (\mathbf{w}, b), and it is bounded below only if the derivative in b vanishes. Setting \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w} - \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{0} and \partial\mathcal{L}/\partial b = -\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0 gives \mathbf{w} = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i and the constraint \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0. Substituting, the term with b disappears (it is multiplied by \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0) and\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 - \mathbf{w}^\top\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i + \sum_i\alpha_i = \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + \sum_i\alpha_i = \sum_i\alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j,

which is the dual objective. No gap. The primal is a convex problem with affine constraints, which is feasible when the data are separable; for such problems strong duality holds (the refined Slater condition), so the maximum of the dual equals the minimum of the primal and a dual solution \hat{\boldsymbol\alpha} exists. At the optimum the minimizer of \mathcal{L}(\cdot, \cdot, \hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}) is the primal solution, which gives \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i, and the equality of the optimal values gives complementary slackness: \tfrac12\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 = \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}, \hat b, \hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}) = \tfrac12\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 - \sum_i\hat\alpha_i[\,y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b) - 1], a sum of non-negative terms that must therefore all vanish. Consequences. (i) is complementary slackness. For (ii), multiply \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i by \hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top: \lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\hat\alpha_i\,y_i\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i = \sum_i\hat\alpha_i(1 - y_i\hat b), using y_i\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i = 1 - y_i\hat b whenever \hat\alpha_i > 0, and \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i = 0 kills the term in \hat b. (iii) and (iv) are read off the formulas. The primal solution is unique because the objective is strictly convex in \mathbf{w}; \hat b is then determined by any support vector, and there is one of each class because \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i = 0 with some \hat\alpha_i > 0 forces both signs to appear. \square

Statement (i) is the sparsity of the SVM: after training, the examples with \hat\alpha_i = 0 could be deleted without changing the classifier. In Worked example 8.1 the dual confirms the guess. Writing \mathbf{w} = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i with the three support vectors, (0, 1) = -\alpha_1(0, 0) - \alpha_2(2, 0) + \alpha_3(1, 2) = (\alpha_3 - 2\alpha_2,\ 2\alpha_3), so \alpha_3 = \tfrac12 and \alpha_2 = \tfrac14; the constraint \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0 gives \alpha_1 = \alpha_3 - \alpha_2 = \tfrac14; and (ii) holds: \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = 1 = \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac12. All the \alpha_i are non-negative and \alpha_4 = \alpha_5 = 0 for the points off the margin, so (\boldsymbol\alpha, \mathbf{w}, b) satisfies all the KKT conditions and, by the theorem, is optimal.

def check_dual(model, X, y):
    """Check the consequences of Theorem 8.2 for a fitted hard-margin linear SVC (y in {-1, +1}),
    comparing with the solution of the primal problem obtained by a general-purpose optimizer."""
    sv = model.support_
    alpha_y = model.dual_coef_.ravel()                       # alpha_i * y_i for the support vectors
    w_dual = alpha_y @ X[sv]                                 # w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i
    cons = [{"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda v, i=i: y[i] * (X[i] @ v[:-1] + v[-1]) - 1} for i in range(len(y))]
    start = np.r_[model.coef_.ravel() * 1.05, model.intercept_]
    primal_sol = minimize(lambda v: 0.5 * v[:-1] @ v[:-1], start, constraints=cons, method="SLSQP", options={"ftol": 1e-14, "maxiter": 1000}).x
    scores = y * model.decision_function(X)
    print(f"  support vectors: {len(sv)} of {len(y)};  largest |w_primal - sum alpha_i y_i x_i| = {np.abs(primal_sol[:-1] - w_dual).max():.1e}")
    print(f"  sum alpha_i y_i = {alpha_y.sum():.1e};  sum alpha_i = {np.abs(alpha_y).sum():.6f};  ||w||^2 = {primal_sol[:-1] @ primal_sol[:-1]:.6f}")
    print(f"  smallest score y_i f(x_i) over the non-support vectors: {np.delete(scores, sv).min():.4f}  (> 1);  scores of the support vectors: "
          f"{scores[sv].min():.4f} to {scores[sv].max():.4f}  (= 1)")


print("Worked example 8.1:")
check_dual(hard_we, X_we, y_we)

Figure 8.1 shows the two problems. In panel (a) the five points of the worked example, the maximum-margin line and the margin hyperplanes. In panel (b), 100 real flowers (setosa and versicolor, petal length and width in centimeters) and the SVM line, drawn with two other separating lines found by the perceptron algorithm from different random orderings of the data: they have zero training error as well, and almost nothing keeps them away from the points.

iris = load_iris()
mask_sv = iris.target < 2                                           # setosa (0) and versicolor (1)
X_ir = iris.data[mask_sv][:, 2:4]                                   # petal length and petal width, in cm
y_ir = 2.0 * iris.target[mask_sv] - 1                               # -1 = setosa, +1 = versicolor
hard_ir = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-10).fit(X_ir, y_ir)
print("Iris setosa/versicolor, hard margin:")
print(f"  w = {hard_ir.coef_.ravel().round(4)}, b = {hard_ir.intercept_[0]:.4f}, margin width 2/||w|| = {2 / np.linalg.norm(hard_ir.coef_):.4f} cm, "
      f"support vectors: examples {hard_ir.support_} (indices from 0)")
check_dual(hard_ir, X_ir, y_ir)
perceptrons = [Perceptron(random_state=s_, max_iter=1000, tol=None, eta0=1.0).fit(X_ir, y_ir) for s_ in (1, 3)]
print("training errors of the two perceptron lines:", [int(np.sum(p.predict(X_ir) != y_ir)) for p in perceptrons])



# Figure 8.1 — the maximum-margin hyperplane: a constructed example and a real one
def figure_8_1():
    def draw_line(ax, w, b, level, **kw):
        xs = np.array(ax.get_xlim())
        if abs(w[1]) > 1e-12:
            ax.plot(xs, (level - b - w[0] * xs) / w[1], **kw)
        else:
            ax.axvline((level - b) / w[0], **kw)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.3))
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.set_xlim(-1, 4.2), ax.set_ylim(-1, 5)
    ax.scatter(*X_we[y_we == -1].T, s=70, color=VERMILION, marker="s", label="$y = -1$")
    ax.scatter(*X_we[y_we == 1].T, s=70, color=BLUE, marker="o", label="$y = +1$")
    ax.scatter(*X_we[hard_we.support_].T, s=260, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=1.6)
    w_, b_ = hard_we.coef_.ravel(), hard_we.intercept_[0]
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, 0, color="k", lw=2)
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, 1, color="k", lw=1.2, ls="--")
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, -1, color="k", lw=1.2, ls="--")
    for i, (px, py) in enumerate(X_we):
        ax.annotate(f"$x_{i + 1}$", (px, py), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 6), fontsize=10)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(2.9, 0.0 + 1.0), xytext=(2.9, 0.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="0.3"))
    ax.text(3.0, 0.45, "margin 1", fontsize=9, color="0.3")
    ax.set(xlabel="$x_1$", ylabel="$x_2$", title="(a) Worked example 8.1: three support vectors")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=9)

    ax = axes[1]
    ax.set_xlim(0.5, 5.3), ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 2.0)
    ax.scatter(*X_ir[y_ir == -1].T, s=22, color=VERMILION, marker="s", label="setosa")
    ax.scatter(*X_ir[y_ir == 1].T, s=22, color=BLUE, marker="o", label="versicolor")
    ax.scatter(*X_ir[hard_ir.support_].T, s=200, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=1.6)
    for p in perceptrons:
        draw_line(ax, p.coef_.ravel(), p.intercept_[0], 0, color="0.55", lw=1.3, ls=":")
    w_, b_ = hard_ir.coef_.ravel(), hard_ir.intercept_[0]
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, 0, color="k", lw=2, label="maximum margin")
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, 1, color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--")
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, -1, color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.plot([], [], color="0.55", ls=":", label="two perceptron lines")
    ax.set(xlabel="petal length (cm)", ylabel="petal width (cm)", title="(b) Iris: two support vectors")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right", fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_1()



Two support vectors, one of each class, determine the line in panel (b), and \hat{\mathbf{w}} is a combination of them only: the other 98 flowers could be removed from the data set without changing the classifier. The numbers above verify the statements of Theorem 8.2 on this real problem: the vector \hat{\mathbf{w}} found by minimizing the primal with a general-purpose optimizer equals \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i computed from the dual coefficients of the solver of scikit-learn, \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0, and \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\alpha_i. The support vectors are the two flowers closest to the other class; the width of the empty strip between the classes is 1.30 cm.

How this relates to Section 7.7.3

Section 7.7.3 computed the same hard-margin direction on the standardized petal measurements by running gradient descent for 

106 steps, and found that its two active examples were the examples with indices 43 and 98 (counting from 0, as Python does). The two computations are not identical, for two reasons that are worth knowing. First, there the intercept was one of the coordinates of \mathbf{w} and was penalized (\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert included it), while the SVM of this chapter leaves b out of the norm: this is also what makes the dual constraint \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0 appear. Second, the standardization changes the geometry of the plane. On the standardized data the two solutions differ by an angle of about 4^\circ in the space of (b, \mathbf{w}), with margins 0.646 (intercept penalized) and 0.658 (intercept free), and the same two support vectors; in the original units the support vectors are the examples 44 and 98. The maximum-margin classifier is not invariant to the scaling of the features (Section 8.7.1).

Z_ir = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_ir)
A_ir = np.c_[np.ones(len(y_ir)), Z_ir]
as_in_ch7 = LinearSVC(C=1e6, loss="hinge", fit_intercept=False, dual=True, max_iter=5_000_000, tol=1e-10).fit(A_ir, y_ir)      # intercept inside the norm
free_b = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-10).fit(Z_ir, y_ir)                                                              # intercept outside the norm
v1 = as_in_ch7.coef_.ravel()
v2 = np.r_[free_b.intercept_, free_b.coef_.ravel()]
print(f"intercept penalized (Chapter 7):  (b, w) = {v1.round(4)}, margin {1 / np.linalg.norm(v1):.4f}, active examples {np.flatnonzero(np.abs(y_ir * (A_ir @ v1) - 1) < 1e-5)}")
print(f"intercept free (this chapter):    (b, w) = {v2.round(4)}, margin {1 / np.linalg.norm(free_b.coef_):.4f}, support vectors {free_b.support_}")
print(f"angle between the two directions: {np.degrees(np.arccos(v1 @ v2 / np.linalg.norm(v1) / np.linalg.norm(v2))):.1f} degrees")

records.content:
The dual of the soft-margin problem differs from that of Theorem 8.2 in a single place: the multipliers are bounded above by C.

Theorem 8.4 (dual problem and KKT conditions of the soft-margin SVM)

The soft-margin primal has a solution and the dual problem\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\ \ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\,y_iy_j\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j
\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad 0\le\alpha_i\le C,\quad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iy_i = 0

has the same optimal value. A primal solution is \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i, and with the margins m_i = y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b) the optimality conditions are\hat\alpha_i = 0\ \Rightarrow\ m_i\ge 1,
\qquad
0 < \hat\alpha_i < C\ \Rightarrow\ m_i = 1,
\qquad
\hat\alpha_i = C\ \Rightarrow\ m_i\le 1,

and these implications are also sufficient. The examples are thus of three kinds: those beyond the margin (\alpha_i = 0, which do not enter \hat{\mathbf{w}}), those exactly on the margin (0 < \alpha_i < C, the free support vectors), and those on or inside the margin or misclassified (\alpha_i = C, the bounded support vectors, with slack \xi_i = 1 - m_i \ge 0). The intercept is obtained from the free support vectors, \hat b = y_k - \hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_k for any free k.

Proof

Attach multipliers \alpha_i\ge 0 to the constraints y_if(\mathbf{x}_i) - 1 + \xi_i\ge 0 and \mu_i\ge 0 to \xi_i\ge 0:\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\xi_i - \sum_i\alpha_i\big[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) - 1 + \xi_i\big] - \sum_i\mu_i\xi_i .

The derivatives with respect to \mathbf{w} and b give, as before, \mathbf{w} = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i and \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0. The derivative with respect to \xi_i is C - \alpha_i - \mu_i = 0, and since \mu_i\ge 0 this means \alpha_i\le C (and \mu_i = C - \alpha_i). Substituting, the terms in \xi_i cancel exactly (C\xi_i - \alpha_i\xi_i - \mu_i\xi_i = 0) and we obtain the same dual function as in Theorem 8.2, now with the box constraint 0\le\alpha_i\le C. The primal is a convex quadratic program with affine constraints and is feasible (take \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}, b = 0, \xi_i = 1), so strong duality holds and the complementary slackness conditions are \alpha_i[\,y_if(\mathbf{x}_i) - 1 + \xi_i] = 0 and \mu_i\xi_i = (C - \alpha_i)\xi_i = 0. If \alpha_i = 0 then \mu_i = C > 0, so \xi_i = 0 and the constraint gives m_i\ge 1. If 0 < \alpha_i < C then \mu_i > 0 forces \xi_i = 0, and \alpha_i > 0 forces the constraint to be active: m_i = 1. If \alpha_i = C then the constraint is active, m_i = 1 - \xi_i\le 1. The sufficiency is the converse of the argument. \square

For C\to\infty the box constraint disappears and the dual becomes the dual of Theorem 8.2. When the data are separable the limit is reached at a finite C: if C_0 is the largest multiplier of the hard-margin solution, every C\ge C_0 gives exactly the same classifier (Exercise 8.4); below C_0 the box constraint becomes active and the solution changes. The cells below show the soft margin on two real problems. The first is the two Iris species that overlap, versicolor and virginica (petal length and width in centimeters), where no hyperplane separates the classes.

mask_vv = iris.target > 0                                                # versicolor (1) and virginica (2)
X_vv = iris.data[mask_vv][:, 2:4]
y_vv = 2.0 * (iris.target[mask_vv] - 1) - 1                              # -1 = versicolor, +1 = virginica

rows, models_vv = [], {}
for C in [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]:
    m_ = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-8).fit(X_vv, y_vv)
    models_vv[C] = m_
    alpha_ = np.abs(m_.dual_coef_.ravel())
    margins_ = y_vv * m_.decision_function(X_vv)
    rows.append({"C": C, "margin width 2/||w||": 2 / np.linalg.norm(m_.coef_), "support vectors": len(m_.support_),
                 "alpha = C": int(np.sum(alpha_ >= C - 1e-8)), "0 < alpha < C": int(np.sum(alpha_ < C - 1e-8)),
                 "margin violators": int(np.sum(margins_ < 1 - 1e-6)), "training errors": int(np.sum(margins_ <= 0))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))



# Figure 8.2 — the soft margin on Iris versicolor/virginica, for three values of C
def figure_8_2():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.6, 3.9), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    xs = np.array([2.9, 7.1])
    for ax, C in zip(axes, [0.01, 1, 100]):
        m_ = models_vv[C]
        w_, b_ = m_.coef_.ravel(), m_.intercept_[0]
        ax.scatter(*X_vv[y_vv == -1].T, s=24, color=VERMILION, marker="s", label="versicolor")
        ax.scatter(*X_vv[y_vv == 1].T, s=24, color=BLUE, marker="o", label="virginica")
        ax.scatter(*X_vv[m_.support_].T, s=120, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=1.0)
        ax.plot(xs, (-b_ - w_[0] * xs) / w_[1], color="k", lw=2)
        for level in (1, -1):
            ax.plot(xs, (level - b_ - w_[0] * xs) / w_[1], color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--")
        ax.set(xlim=(2.9, 7.1), ylim=(0.9, 2.65), xlabel="petal length (cm)",
               title=f"$C = {C:g}$: {len(m_.support_)} support vectors")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("petal width (cm)")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_2()



The progression is the one of Chapter 6. With a small C the margin is wide, nearly all the examples are inside it (they are support vectors with \alpha_i = C) and the line is determined by the bulk of the data. With a large C the margin shrinks around a few examples near the boundary, the number of support vectors falls, and the line follows the overlap region more closely. The support vectors are not only the examples that are “hard”, but all those that are on or beyond the wrong side of their margin: for a small C they are the majority. The number of support vectors is a measure of the complexity of the solution, as we shall see in Section 8.6.

The second problem is the Breast Cancer training set, standardized, with C = 1 (the value that Section 6.5 selected for the logistic regression). The cell checks the conditions of Theorem 8.4, computes the primal objective \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\xi_i and the dual objective \sum_i\alpha_i - \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 from the solution of the solver, and shows what happens at the transition to the hard margin.

bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
Xb = bc.data.to_numpy()
yb = (1 - bc.target).to_numpy().astype(int)                              # malignant = 1, as in Chapters 6 and 7
Xb_tr, Xb_te, yb_tr, yb_te = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=yb)
scaler_b = StandardScaler().fit(Xb_tr)
Zb, Zb_te = scaler_b.transform(Xb_tr), scaler_b.transform(Xb_te)
sb, sb_te = 2.0 * yb_tr - 1, 2.0 * yb_te - 1                             # labels in {-1, +1}
n_b = len(sb)
print(f"Breast Cancer: {n_b} training patients, {Zb.shape[1]} features (standardized), {len(sb_te)} test patients; malignant = +1")


def dual_variables(model, n):
    alpha = np.zeros(n)
    alpha[model.support_] = np.abs(model.dual_coef_.ravel())
    return alpha


C_b = 1.0
svm_b = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C_b, tol=1e-9).fit(Zb, sb)
alpha_b = dual_variables(svm_b, n_b)
m_b = sb * svm_b.decision_function(Zb)                                   # margins y_i f(x_i)
w_b = svm_b.coef_.ravel()
kinds = {"alpha = 0 (beyond the margin)": alpha_b <= 1e-9,
         "0 < alpha < C (on the margin)": (alpha_b > 1e-9) & (alpha_b < C_b - 1e-6),
         "alpha = C (inside, or misclassified)": alpha_b >= C_b - 1e-6}
rows = [{"kind": k, "examples": int(v.sum()), "smallest margin": m_b[v].min(), "largest margin": m_b[v].max(), "misclassified": int((m_b[v] <= 0).sum())}
        for k, v in kinds.items()]
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
slack = np.maximum(0, 1 - m_b)
primal_value = 0.5 * w_b @ w_b + C_b * slack.sum()
dual_value = alpha_b.sum() - 0.5 * w_b @ w_b
print(f"primal objective {primal_value:.6f}, dual objective {dual_value:.6f}; sum of alpha_i y_i = {alpha_b @ sb:.1e}; "
      f"test accuracy {np.mean(np.sign(svm_b.decision_function(Zb_te)) == sb_te):.4f}")

hard_b = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-9).fit(Zb, sb)
C0 = np.abs(hard_b.dual_coef_).max()
print(f"hard margin: {len(hard_b.support_)} support vectors, ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(hard_b.coef_):.3f}, largest multiplier C0 = {C0:.2f}")
for factor in [0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 10]:
    m_ = SVC(kernel="linear", C=factor * C0, tol=1e-9).fit(Zb, sb)
    diff = np.linalg.norm(m_.coef_ - hard_b.coef_) / np.linalg.norm(hard_b.coef_)
    print(f"  C = {factor:>4} * C0 = {factor * C0:7.2f}: ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(m_.coef_):7.3f}, relative distance from the hard-margin w = {diff:.1e}")





# Figure 8.3 — the dual variables against the margins, Breast Cancer, C = 1
def figure_8_3():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))
    styles = [("alpha = 0 (beyond the margin)", GREEN, "o"), ("0 < alpha < C (on the margin)", BLUE, "s"), ("alpha = C (inside, or misclassified)", VERMILION, "^")]
    labels = [r"$\alpha_i = 0$: beyond the margin", r"$0 < \alpha_i < C$: on the margin", r"$\alpha_i = C$: inside it or misclassified"]
    for (k, color, marker), lab in zip(styles, labels):
        v = kinds[k]
        ax.scatter(m_b[v], alpha_b[v], s=28, color=color, marker=marker, label=f"{lab} ({v.sum()})", alpha=0.85)
    ax.axvline(1, color="0.4", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.axvline(0, color="0.4", lw=1, ls=":")
    ax.axhline(C_b, color="0.4", lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.text(1.12, 0.52, "$m_i = 1$", fontsize=9, color="0.3")
    ax.text(0.03, 0.52, "$m_i = 0$", fontsize=9, color="0.3")
    ax.text(2.6, C_b + 0.025, "$\\alpha_i = C$", fontsize=9, color="0.3")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"margin $m_i = y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)$", ylabel=r"dual variable $\alpha_i$", xlim=(-3.5, 6.5), ylim=(-0.04, 1.12),
           title="Breast Cancer, $C = 1$: the three kinds of examples")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, loc="center right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_3()



The 426 patients fall in the three kinds of Theorem 8.4 exactly as stated: 390 are beyond the margin (\alpha_i = 0; the smallest margin among them is 1.018 and the largest 31.5), 20 are exactly on it (0 < \alpha_i < C; all with margin 1.0000), and 16 have \alpha_i = C, with margins from -3.10 to 0.87, four of them misclassified. So 36 of the 426 examples (8.5\%) determine \hat{\mathbf{w}}, and 390 could be deleted without changing the classifier. The primal and dual objectives agree (19.0303 and 19.0303, up to the tolerance of the solver) and \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0. The test accuracy is 0.958 (6 errors among 143 patients). The last lines show the transition to the hard margin: its solution has 24 support vectors and \lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert = 28.4, the value that appeared in Exercise 7.10 (there the intercept was part of the norm), and its largest multiplier is C_0 = 125. For every C\ge C_0 the soft-margin solution is exactly the hard-margin one (relative distance 

10-11 or zero), while at 0.9\,C_0 it is already 8\% away and at C_0/4, 59\% away, with a norm of 13.6. The value C = 1 that works well in practice is two orders of magnitude below C_0 and has \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 2.7: the hard margin is the far end of a path, not the typical SVM.

records.content:
All the classifiers of Chapters 6 to 8 minimize an average of a loss of the margin m = y\,f(\mathbf{x}) plus a penalty, and differ only in the loss. Figure 8.4 draws four of them as functions of m: the 0–1 loss \mathbb{I}[m\le 0] that we would like to minimize but cannot (it is not convex, nor continuous), the hinge loss \max\{0, 1 - m\} of this chapter, its square \max\{0, 1 - m\}^2 (the loss of LinearSVC by default, which is differentiable), and the logistic loss \log_2(1 + e^{-m}) of Chapter 6 (divided by \ln 2 so that it passes through the point (0, 1) like the others).

# Figure 8.4 — four losses as functions of the margin
def figure_8_4():
    m = np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 600)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
    ax.plot(m, (m <= 0).astype(float), color="k", lw=2, label="0–1 loss")
    ax.plot(m, np.maximum(0, 1 - m), color=BLUE, lw=2.2, label="hinge loss")
    ax.plot(m, np.maximum(0, 1 - m) ** 2, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, ls="--", label="squared hinge loss")
    ax.plot(m, np.log2(1 + np.exp(-m)), color=VERMILION, lw=2.2, ls="-.", label=r"logistic loss, $\log_2(1 + e^{-m})$")
    ax.axvline(1, color="0.6", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"margin $m = y\,f(\mathbf{x})$", ylabel="loss", xlim=(-2.2, 2.2), ylim=(-0.05, 3.3), title="Surrogates of the 0–1 loss")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_4()



The hinge, the squared hinge and the logistic loss are convex upper bounds of the 0–1 loss, which makes them tractable surrogates (the hinge loss is the one that appears in the margin bound of Section 3.8.4 through the ramp loss \varphi_\gamma, which it dominates). The difference that matters is at the right of the plot: the hinge loss is exactly zero for m\ge 1, so an example that is well classified with a margin of at least one has no influence on the solution (it has \alpha_i = 0), while the logistic loss is positive for every margin and every example keeps pulling on the weights, ever more weakly. This is the origin of the sparsity of the SVM. To compare the two precisely, return to the stationarity condition of the regularized logistic regression of Section 6.5, written in the scikit-learn parametrization where the objective is \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\log(1 + e^{-m_i}). Setting the gradient in \mathbf{w} and in b to zero gives\mathbf{w} = \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,y_i\,\mathbf{x}_i,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iy_i = 0,
\qquad
\boxed{\ \alpha_i^{\text{logistic}} = C\,\sigma(-m_i)\ }

with \sigma the sigmoid. The logistic regression has the same representation as the SVM, as a combination of the training examples with weights \alpha_i\in(0, C) and \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0; the difference is only the rule that gives the weights. For the hinge loss the rule is \alpha_i = C if m_i < 1, \alpha_i = 0 if m_i > 1 and \alpha_i\in[0, C] if m_i = 1: a step function of the margin, which is a hardened version of the smooth sigmoid C\sigma(-m_i). We can check the identity on the Breast Cancer data.

logit_b = LogisticRegression(C=C_b, tol=1e-12, max_iter=100_000).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
w_l, b_l = logit_b.coef_.ravel(), logit_b.intercept_[0]
m_l = sb * (Zb @ w_l + b_l)
alpha_l = C_b / (1 + np.exp(m_l))                                         # C * sigmoid(-m_i)
print(f"logistic regression, C = {C_b}: largest |w - sum alpha_i y_i x_i| = {np.abs(w_l - (alpha_l * sb) @ Zb).max():.1e}, sum alpha_i y_i = {alpha_l @ sb:.1e}")
cosine = w_b @ w_l / (np.linalg.norm(w_b) * np.linalg.norm(w_l))
print(f"cosine between the SVM weights and the logistic weights: {cosine:.4f};  norms {np.linalg.norm(w_b):.3f} and {np.linalg.norm(w_l):.3f}")
print(f"examples with a non-zero multiplier: SVM {int((alpha_b > 1e-9).sum())} of {n_b};  "
      f"logistic: {int((alpha_l > 1e-3 * C_b).sum())} with alpha_i > 0.001 C, {int((alpha_l > 1e-6 * C_b).sum())} with alpha_i > 1e-6 C, {int((alpha_l > 0).sum())} with alpha_i > 0")
print(f"test accuracy: SVM {np.mean(np.sign(svm_b.decision_function(Zb_te)) == sb_te):.4f}, logistic {logit_b.score(Zb_te, yb_te):.4f}")



The identity holds to the precision of the solver (2\cdot 10^{-6}): the regularized logistic regression is also a combination of training examples with \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0, but no multiplier is exactly zero. For the same C = 1 the logistic regression has 228 examples with \alpha_i > 0.001\,C and 387 with \alpha_i > 10^{-6}C, against 36 for the SVM (20 free and 16 bounded). The two weight vectors point in similar directions (cosine 0.919; norms 2.71 for the SVM and 3.76 for the logistic regression) and give the same kind of accuracy on the test set, 0.958 and 0.965 (6 and 5 errors among 143 patients). The difference between the two methods is therefore not in what they can express but in how the training set is used: the SVM needs only its support vectors, which gives a compact model and the leave-one-out bound of Section 8.6, while the logistic regression keeps a small weight on every example and delivers probabilities. When the data are separable and C\to\infty, the direction of the logistic solution converges to the hard-margin direction (Section 7.7.3 reached it from the side of gradient descent), because the margins of the non-support examples grow, so that their weights C\sigma(-m_i) vanish.
