Panel (b) of Figure 10.13 is the answer. The naive p-value of the best of ten features is below 0.05 in 32\% of the shuffles (for ten independent features it would be 1-0.95^{10}=40\%; the features are correlated, which lowers the rate) and its mean is 0.12 instead of 0.5: the distribution piles up at zero. With data splitting the rate is 5.8\%, close to the nominal 5\% (the Monte Carlo error is 0.3 points, and the t distribution is only approximately valid for the skewed response of Diabetes), and the p-values are uniform, with mean 0.49. The price of data splitting is half of the data for each step; the point is that selection and testing must not use the same data.

The rule that follows is the one of Section 2.7 with a higher price. Everything that looks at the labels belongs inside the loop: the choice of \lambda (and \alpha) by cross-validation, the selector of a filter, the elimination steps of RFE, the refit on the selected support. If the final model is also to be evaluated, the loop must be nested (Section 5.4.3): an inner cross-validation chooses \lambda on the training part of each outer fold, and the outer fold, never seen by the inner one, estimates the error. In code,pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SelectFromModel(LassoCV(cv=5)), Ridge(alpha=1.0))
score = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0))

estimates the error of the whole procedure “choose \lambda by cross-validation, keep the features with non-zero weights, fit a ridge on them”, every step of which sees only the training part of each fold. What the pipeline does not give is a valid confidence statement about the selected coefficients (their standard errors and p-values), which needs methods designed for it: data splitting as above, or the post-selection inference of Lee, Sun, Sun and Taylor (2016) in the further reading.

Sparse models (Section 10.2). A sparse model uses few of the p features (\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0=s non-zero weights). The reasons are interpretation, cost and, when p is large compared with n, estimation error: least squares pays \sigma^2p/n (Theorem 6.1) and a model that knows the support pays \sigma^2 s/n. The number of supports is \binom ps: 1.7\times10^{13} for p=100, s=10.

Best subset (Section 10.3). On the ten Diabetes features the exhaustive search takes a fraction of a second. The training error falls with the size (\mathrm{RSS} is nested, Proposition 10.1) and cannot choose it; C_p, the BIC and cross-validation choose 7, 6 and 7 features, and the one-standard-error rule 5 (sex, bmi, bp, s3, s5). The effective degrees of freedom of a searched subset exceed its size (Proposition 10.2): the best single feature out of ten has 3.4, not 1. Forward selection finds the best subset for sizes 1 to 5 and 9 and 10 and misses it for 6 to 8.

Greedy pursuit (Section 10.4). OMP recovers the true support if the exact recovery condition holds (Theorem 10.4), and in particular if the coherence satisfies \mu(2s-1)<1 (Corollary 10.5). On the real, correlated Diabetes features the coherence is 0.893 and the conditions are vacuous; on a Gaussian design OMP needs more examples than the oracle lasso path to recover the support (n=30: 0.73 against 1.00).

The lasso (Section 10.5). The \ell_1 penalty is the convex relaxation of \lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0, and its ball has corners on the axes, where the solutions are. For an orthonormal design the solution is soft-thresholding (Proposition 10.6); in general it is characterized by \frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}=\lambda\operatorname{sign}(w_j) on the active set and \lvert\frac1n\mathbf{x}_j^\top\mathbf{r}\rvert\le\lambda off it (Theorem 10.7), which gives \lambda_{\max}=\frac1n\lVert\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\rVert_\infty (45.97 on Diabetes). The path is piecewise linear with 15 knots for 10 features and is not monotone: s2 and s3 leave the model and re-enter. The penalty is a Laplace prior, and it biases the non-zero weights toward zero (Section 10.5.6).

Algorithms (Section 10.6). Coordinate descent (Proposition 10.8) is exact in each step and reaches 

10-9 in 15 sweeps; proximal gradient (ISTA, Proposition 10.9, Theorem 10.10, rate O(1/k)) needs 92 iterations and FISTA gains only at low accuracy, because the problem restricted to the active set is well conditioned (\kappa_S\approx5 against \kappa=418). The subgradient method never reaches 

10-3 after 2,000 iterations and never produces a zero. The path with warm starts is the standard way to compute the lasso.

Choosing \lambda and what it buys (Section 10.7). Cross-validation gives nine features at the minimum and five at the one-SE value, the same five as best subset. The degrees of freedom of the lasso equal the expected number of non-zero weights (Proposition 10.11 in the orthonormal case, checked by Monte Carlo on the real design). On the test patients all methods are within 0.9 RMSE points and, over 30 splits, least squares, ridge and the lasso are indistinguishable (54.9, 55.0, 54.9): sparsity costs nothing in prediction and gains nothing when p=10 and n=331; the one-SE rule costs about 1.3 points for 4.6 features instead of 8.2, a difference the data do not resolve. The quadratic features do not help either (the single-split gain of 2.2 points vanishes over 30 splits). The benefit of \ell_1 appears when most features are useless: with 1,000 noise columns ridge goes from 56.4 to 72.8 and the lasso from 56.9 to 60.6, in agreement with the slow-rate bound (Theorem 10.12), in which the number of features enters only through \ln p.

Elastic net (Section 10.8). Adding a ridge penalty gives a strictly convex problem, solved by any lasso solver on augmented data (Proposition 10.13), and the grouping effect (Theorem 10.14): two selected features with correlation \rho differ by at most \frac{\lVert\mathbf{y}\rVert}{\sqrt n\lambda_2}\sqrt{2(1-\rho)}. Where the lasso, on a feature and its noisy twin, keeps only one of the two in 67\% of the bootstrap samples, the elastic net keeps both in all of them and with almost equal weights. The selected sets of the elastic net are more reproducible between five and eight features, though not uniformly, and reproducible is not the same as true.

Sparse classification (Section 10.9). The \ell_1-penalized logistic regression has its own \lambda_{\max} (Proposition 10.15). On Breast Cancer it matches ridge on prediction (3 to 5 errors in 143, indistinguishable) and keeps 12 of the 30 features, which are correlated versions of 10 measurements. For the \ell_2 penalty the weights lie in the row space of the data (Theorem 9.4); for \ell_1 they do not (43\% of the length of the weights lies outside it on n=40 images of Digits): the kernel trick does not apply.

Filters, wrappers, embedded (Section 10.10). A filter judges each feature alone and keeps redundant ones (three of its five Breast Cancer features measure the size of the nucleus); with the selection inside the folds, at five features its cross-validated log loss is 0.145 against 0.109 for RFE and 0.110 for the \ell_1 selection, and the three families agree again from twenty features on.

Selection inside the loop (Section 10.11). On shuffled labels, selecting five features out of 564 on all the data and then cross-validating gives an accuracy of 0.81 for a classifier with no information, against 0.497 with the selection inside each fold; the naive p-value of the best of ten features is below 0.05 in 32\% of the shuffles, and 5.8\% with data splitting. Everything that looks at the labels belongs inside the loop (choice of \lambda, selector, refit); evaluating the whole procedure needs a nested loop.

Where this leaves gradient methods (Section 7.7.2). Early stopping of gradient descent acts like an \ell_2 penalty; the analogue for \ell_1 is stagewise forward selection with tiny steps, whose path approximates the lasso path (Efron et al., 2004, in the further reading). Plain gradient descent on the lasso objective is not an option because of the kink at zero: the proximal and coordinate methods exist for that reason.

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in 

Appendix C.

Exercise 10.1 ★ — Four estimators by hand. (Constructed numbers.) For an orthonormal design, \frac1n\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{I}, the least-squares weights are \hat{\mathbf{w}}^{\rm ols}=(4, -2.5, 1.2, -0.6, 0.2). Write the weights of (a) the lasso with \lambda=1, (b) ridge regression with \lambda_2=1, (c) best subset of size 2, (d) the elastic net with \lambda_1=\lambda_2=1. (e) For which values of \lambda does the lasso keep exactly two weights, and by how much are they biased with respect to those of (c)?

Hint. The lasso is S_\lambda(\hat w^{\rm ols}_j) (Proposition 10.6), ridge is \hat w^{\rm ols}_j/(1+\lambda_2), best subset keeps the two largest in absolute value; for (d) use Exercise 10.4.

Exercise 10.2 ★★ — A two-feature lasso path. (Constructed numbers.) Standardized features with \frac1n\mathbf{z}_1^\top\mathbf{z}_2=\rho=0.5 and \frac1n\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{y}=(c_1,c_2)=(0.8,0.6). (a) Find \lambda_{\max} and the first feature to enter. (b) Find the value of \lambda at which the second feature enters, and the weights for every \lambda from \lambda_{\max} down to 0; check that they reach the least-squares solution. (c) Repeat (b) with c_2=0.3: when does the second feature enter, with which sign, and how does this compare with the sign changes of s3 along the path of Figure 10.5?

Hint. With only feature 1 active, \hat w_1=c_1-\lambda. Feature 2 enters when \lvert c_2-\rho\hat w_1\rvert=\lambda (Theorem 10.7). With both active solve \begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{c}-\lambda\,\mathbf{s} with the signs \mathbf{s}.

Exercise 10.3 ★★ — Repeated columns. Let two columns of \mathbf{Z} be identical, \mathbf{z}_j=\mathbf{z}_k. (a) Show that the data term of the objective depends on w_j and w_k only through w_j+w_k. (b) Show that if \hat{\mathbf{w}} is a lasso solution with \hat w_j\hat w_k\ge0, then moving weight between the two coordinates, keeping their sum and their sign, gives other solutions: the set of lasso solutions contains a segment. (c) Show that the elastic net with \lambda_2>0 has the unique solution \hat w_j=\hat w_k, and say how this agrees with Theorem 10.14.

Hint. (b) \lvert w_j\rvert+\lvert w_k\rvert=\lvert w_j+w_k\rvert when the two have the same sign. (c) For a fixed sum s=w_j+w_k, w_j^2+w_k^2\ge s^2/2 with equality only at w_j=w_k.

Exercise 10.4 ★★ — The elastic net for an orthonormal design. With \frac1n\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{I}, (a) show that the elastic net solution is \hat w_j = S_{\lambda_1}(\hat w_j^{\rm ols})/(1+\lambda_2). (b) Show that the factor 1+\lambda_2 is a second shrinkage on top of that of the lasso, and that in this case the elastic net rescaled by 1+\lambda_2 is the lasso with the same \lambda_1. (c) Explain why this does not contradict Theorem 10.14: what does the grouping effect need that an orthonormal design does not have?

Hint. The objective separates by coordinates: minimize \frac12(w-a)^2+\lambda_1\lvert w\rvert+\frac{\lambda_2}2w^2, i.e. \frac{1+\lambda_2}{2}\big(w-\frac a{1+\lambda_2}\big)^2+\lambda_1\lvert w\rvert+{\rm const}.

Exercise 10.5 ★★★ — The lasso path is piecewise linear. Let A be the active set and \mathbf{s}_A the signs on an interval of \lambda over which neither changes. (a) Show that on the interval \hat{\mathbf{w}}_A(\lambda)=\boldsymbol\theta-\lambda\mathbf{u} with \boldsymbol\theta=(\frac1n\mathbf{Z}_A^\top\mathbf{Z}_A)^{-1}\frac1n\mathbf{Z}_A^\top\mathbf{y} and \mathbf{u}=(\frac1n\mathbf{Z}_A^\top\mathbf{Z}_A)^{-1}\mathbf{s}_A. (b) Give the value of \lambda at which an inactive feature j enters, and the value at which an active feature k leaves. (c) Apply the formulas to Exercise 10.2 and recover the knots. (d) Explain why the number of knots can exceed p (the Diabetes path had 15 knots for 10 features).

Hint. (a) is (10.5) on the active set. (b) For j\notin A the correlation with the residual is c_j(\lambda)=a_j+\lambda b_j, affine in \lambda, with a_j=\frac1n\mathbf{z}_j^\top(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{Z}_A\boldsymbol\theta) and b_j=\frac1n\mathbf{z}_j^\top\mathbf{Z}_A\mathbf{u}; it enters when c_j=\pm\lambda. An active coordinate leaves when \theta_k-\lambda u_k=0. (d) Features may leave and re-enter.

Exercise 10.6 ★ — The lasso on Wine. Use the Wine data (load_wine) as a regression problem: predict alcohol from the other 12 features, with a 75\%/25\% split (random_state=SEED) and the features standardized with the training statistics. (a) Compute the lasso path with lasso_path and plot it. (b) Choose \lambda by 10-fold cross-validation (minimum and one-SE rule) and by the AIC and the BIC (LassoLarsIC); list the selected features for each. (c) Compare the test RMSE of least squares, ridge (RidgeCV) and the two lasso models, and verify the optimality conditions of Theorem 10.7 for the lasso at the CV minimum.

Hint. LassoCV(alphas=100) gives the grid and mse_path_; the one-SE rule needs the mean and standard error across folds; the KKT check is \frac1n\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{r}=\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}) on the active set and \lvert\frac1n\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{r}\rvert\le\lambda elsewhere.

Exercise 10.7 ★★ — Elastic net by coordinate descent. Implement cyclic coordinate descent for the elastic net, with the update w_j\leftarrow S_{\lambda_1}(\rho_j)/(1+\lambda_2) (\rho_j the partial-residual correlation, Proposition 10.8 and Exercise 10.4), and the objective gap as the stopping rule. (a) Check it against ElasticNet on the Wine problem of Exercise 10.6. (b) On the 65 quadratic features of Diabetes (standardized, the 331 training patients), count the sweeps needed to bring the gap below 

10-10 for \lambda_2\in\{0, 0.1, 1\} with \lambda_1=1. Why does the number decrease with \lambda_2?

Hint. Keep the residual up to date: after changing w_j by \delta, subtract \delta\,\mathbf{z}_j from it. The extra term adds \lambda_2 to the smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian, which makes the problem strongly convex (Theorem 7.5).

Exercise 10.8 ★★ — Noise columns on Wine. On the Wine regression of Exercise 10.6, append m\in\{0, 10, 100, 1000\} columns of Gaussian noise (a constructed addition, as in Section 4.7.2) and compare, over 20 random splits, least squares (when p<n_{\rm train}), ridge, the lasso at its CV minimum and the elastic net with \ell_1 ratio 0.5, all with \lambda chosen by 5-fold cross-validation: test RMSE, and the number of noise columns selected. Does the error of the lasso grow with \ln p rather than with p, as Theorem 10.12 suggests?

Hint. ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=0.5, cv=5); plot the RMSE against \ln(12+m) and against 12+m; the noise is generated once per split and the columns are standardized with the training statistics.

Exercise 10.9 ★★★ — Stability selection. On the 331 Diabetes training patients with 20 appended noise columns (constructed), (a) fit the lasso at the one-SE value of \lambda of the full training set on 100 random half-samples (drawn without replacement) and record the selection frequency of each of the 30 columns; (b) keep the columns with frequency at least 0.7 and count the real features and the noise columns selected, and compare with the lasso at the one-SE value fitted once on the full training set; (c) repeat with the elastic net with \ell_1 ratio 0.5, whose penalty is chosen by the one-SE rule on the full training set too. Which noise columns does each method select, and how often?

Hint. Meinshausen and Bühlmann (2010) show that the expected number of false selections is bounded when the frequency threshold and the number of selections per half-sample are controlled; here we only measure it. Use rng.choice(n, n // 2, replace=False).

Exercise 10.10 ★★★ — The winner’s curse of \lambda. Take 60 random patients of Diabetes, append 200 noise columns (constructed) and shuffle the response, so that no feature carries information. (a) For 30 repetitions compute the minimum of the cross-validated error of LassoCV over the grid of \lambda (the number that people usually report) and compare it with the error of the null model, the variance of the response. (b) Estimate the error of the whole procedure “choose \lambda by 5-fold cross-validation, fit the lasso” by an outer 5-fold cross-validation with LassoCV inside it (nested), and compare. Which of the two is honest, and what does the other one say about the winner’s curse of Section 5.4.3?

Hint. With no signal the best achievable mean squared error is the variance of the response; any estimate below it is optimistic. In the nested loop LassoCV is fitted only on the training part of each outer fold.

We have now seen two ways to control a linear model with many features: shrinking all the weights (ridge) and setting most of them to zero (the \ell_1 penalty and the selection methods built on it). Both keep the model linear in the features, and both make the same assumption, that the effect of a feature is the same everywhere in the data. Chapter 11 abandons it. A decision tree splits the feature space into boxes by a sequence of thresholds on single features, and in doing so selects features adaptively, region by region, ignores irrelevant ones without a penalty (the observation of Section 4.7.2 turned into a method), and needs no scaling (the lesson of Section 9.6.4 and Exercise 9.8). Single trees have high variance, and the remedy is the subject of the second half of the chapter: bagging, random forests and boosting, the last being gradient descent in a space of functions (the loop of Chapter 7, with trees as the steps). Their probabilities are typically badly calibrated, which is the situation of Sections 5.6.4 and 8.7.3, and the feature importances that forests report face the problem of this chapter again: correlated features share the credit, and selecting on the importance outside the loop leaks the labels.

Each technical chapter follows the same structure, so that you always know where to look:

Each technical chapter is a Jupyter notebook that combines text, equations, code, outputs, and figures. There are two ways to use it:

Read it online. The published website contains the chapters with all outputs and figures already computed, so you can read the book without installing anything.

Datasets are loaded with library functions rather than from files you have to find. Some of them, for example the image datasets of torchvision, are downloaded automatically the first time you run a notebook, so you need an internet connection once.

The notebooks are designed to run on an ordinary computer. A GPU makes the deep learning chapters faster but is not required.

Python (computational) exercises are solved on the computer, usually with a real dataset. They train you to implement, experiment, and interpret.

★★ Core: applies the chapter’s ideas to a new but similar situation.

★★★ Challenge: combines several ideas or asks you to explore. It is meant to be demanding, not impossible.

Exercises are different from the worked examples, which are solved completely in the text. For each exercise you will find hints after the statement, and complete solutions or detailed solution outlines are collected in Appendix C. Try the exercise before reading the hints, and read the hints before looking at the solution.

Derive once by hand. Follow each derivation on paper at least once. Writing the steps yourself is the best way to understand them.

Predict, then run. Before executing a cell, guess what it will output. When the result surprises you, you have found something worth understanding.

Change things. Modify a hyperparameter, a dataset, or a line of code, and observe the effect. The notebooks are meant to be altered.

Move between math and code. When you read a formula, find the line of code that implements it, and the other way around.

A Hands-On Mathematical Guide with Jupyter Notebooks, scikit-learn and PyTorch

Mario Medone

Version 0.10.0 · 2026

Machine learning is built on ideas that every student of linear algebra and calculus already knows: vectors, matrices, projections, eigenvalues, gradients and the chain rule. This book shows how those ideas become working algorithms, starting from nearest neighbors and regularized least squares, passing through kernels, clustering and PCA, and arriving at deep networks, transformers and generative models.

Every chapter pairs mathematics with code. Derivations are written out step by step, every method is implemented in Python on real datasets taken from standard libraries, and each chapter closes with exercises of increasing difficulty, both by hand and on the computer. The chapters are Jupyter notebooks, so you can re-run every computation, change it, and see what happens.
This book is a work in progress and is published one chapter at a time. Each release has a version number, and version 1.0.0 will mark the complete book. The current version is 0.10.0.

Read online: 

https://​brosss98​.github​.io​/machine​-learning​-with​-python​-book/

Source code and notebooks: 

https://​github​.com​/Brosss98​/machine​-learning​-with​-python​-book

Report an error or suggest an improvement: 

https://​github​.com​/Brosss98​/machine​-learning​-with​-python​-book​/issues

Copyright and Editorial Information for the details.
This page collects the notation used throughout the book. Do not try to memorize it: each symbol is introduced again where it first appears, and you can return here whenever you need.

Symbol

Meaning

n

Number of samples (examples)

d

Number of features (input dimension)

K

Number of classes or clusters

\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^d

The i-th input vector

y_i

The label or target of the i-th example

\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}

Data matrix: its i-th row is \mathbf{x}_i^\top

\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}

Vector of all targets

S=\{(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}

Training set

In code, the data matrix is an array X of shape (n, d), with one sample per row, which is the convention of scikit-learn.

Symbol

Meaning

f

A prediction function; \hat{y}=f(\mathbf{x}) is the prediction for \mathbf{x}

\mathcal{H}

Hypothesis space: the set of functions a method can choose from

\mathbf{w},\ b

Weights and bias of a model

\boldsymbol{\theta}

Generic vector of parameters

\ell(y,\hat{y})

Loss on a single example

R(f)

Expected risk of f

\hat{R}_S(f)

Empirical risk of f on the training set S

\lambda

Regularization strength

\eta

Learning rate

\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L

Gradient of the function L with respect to \mathbf{w}

\operatorname{argmin}_{\mathbf{w}}\, L(\mathbf{w})

The value of \mathbf{w} that minimizes L

Symbol

Meaning

f^\ast,\ R^\ast

Bayes predictor and Bayes risk: the smallest risk of any function

\eta(\mathbf{x})

Regression function \mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}] (for y\in\{0,1\} it is \mathbb{P}(y=1\mid\mathbf{x})); not the learning rate

\hat f_S

The function chosen by empirical risk minimization on the training set S

f_{\mathcal{H}}

The best function in \mathcal{H}, that is, the one with the smallest expected risk

\varepsilon,\ \delta

Accuracy and failure probability of a guarantee: “with probability at least 1-\delta, the error is at most \varepsilon”

\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(n)

Growth function: the largest number of labelings of n points that \mathcal{H} can produce

d_{\mathrm{VC}}

Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension: the size of the largest set of points that \mathcal{H} can label in all possible ways

\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}),\ \mathfrak{R}_n(\mathcal{F})

Empirical and expected Rademacher complexity of a class \mathcal{F}

Symbol

Meaning

N_k(\mathbf{x})

The set of the k training points nearest to \mathbf{x} (its k nearest neighbors)

\hat f_k(\mathbf{x})

The prediction of the k-nearest-neighbor method at \mathbf{x}

f

The true regression function, f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y\mid\mathbf{x}] (the function called \eta in Chapter 3)

\sigma^2

Variance of the noise, y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon

\text{bias}^2,\ \text{variance}

Squared systematic error and sensitivity to the training set of a prediction \hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0): \mathbb{E}[(y_0-\hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0))^2]=\sigma^2+\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}

Symbol

Meaning

K,\ \kappa(i)

Number of folds of cross-validation; the index of the fold that contains example i

\mathrm{CV}_K

The K-fold cross-validation estimate of the error: the average loss of each example under the model fitted without its fold

n_{\mathrm{val}},\ m

Size of a validation set; number of candidate models or configurations among which the best is selected

\mathrm{TP},\ \mathrm{FP},\ \mathrm{FN},\ \mathrm{TN}

Entries of the confusion matrix: true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives

\text{TPR}(t),\ \text{FPR}(t)

True-positive rate (recall) and false-positive rate of the rule “predict positive if the score is at least t”

S^+,\ S^-

Score of a randomly chosen positive and of a randomly chosen negative example

\text{AUC},\ \text{AP}

Area under the ROC curve; average precision (area under the precision–recall curve)

F_\beta

Weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall; \beta > 1 gives more weight to recall

\pi

Prevalence: the fraction of positive examples in the population

c_{FP},\ c_{FN},\ t^\ast

Costs of a false positive and of a false negative; the cost-optimal threshold t^\ast = c_{FP}/(c_{FP}+c_{FN}) for calibrated probabilities

h_{ii}

Leverage of example i in linear regression (diagonal of the hat matrix); the leave-one-out residual is e_i/(1-h_{ii})

Symbol

Meaning

\lambda,\ \hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambda

Strength of the \ell_2 penalty and the ridge estimator, which minimizes \lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 (alpha in scikit-learn’s Ridge); for logistic regression the objective is the mean loss plus \tfrac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2. The intercept is never penalized

\sigma_j,\ \mathbf{u}_j,\ \mathbf{v}_j,\ f_j(\lambda)

Singular values and left and right singular vectors of the centered feature matrix; shrinkage factors f_j(\lambda)=\sigma_j^2/(\sigma_j^2+\lambda) of ridge. (Do not confuse \sigma_j with \sigma^2, the noise variance, nor with \sigma(\cdot), the sigmoid)

\mathbf{H}_\lambda,\ \mathrm{df}(\lambda)

Smoother (hat) matrix of ridge, \hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{H}_\lambda\mathbf{y}, and effective degrees of freedom \mathrm{df}(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{H}_\lambda=\sum_jf_j(\lambda) (plus 1 for the intercept)

\mathrm{VIF}_j

Variance inflation factor of feature j, 1/(1-R_j^2) with R_j^2 the R^2 of regressing feature j on the others

\sigma(z)

Logistic function (sigmoid) 1/(1+e^{-z}); the log-odds \log\frac{\eta}{1-\eta} are linear in the features

\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\ \boldsymbol\theta

Design matrix with a column of ones in front, and the parameter vector (b,\mathbf{w}) that includes the intercept

p_i,\ \mathbf{S}

Predicted probability of class 1 for example i; the diagonal matrix \mathbf{S}=\mathrm{diag}\big(p_i(1-p_i)\big) of the Newton weights. (Elsewhere in the chapter p is the number of parameters)

m_i,\ L,\ J_\lambda

Signed score m_i=(2y_i-1)z_i; negative log-likelihood (log-loss, cross-entropy) L=\sum_i\log(1+e^{-m_i}); penalized objective J_\lambda

C

Inverse regularization strength of scikit-learn: C multiplies the sum of the losses, so \lambda=1/(Cn)

K,\ p_k(\mathbf{x}),\ \mathbf{w}_k,\ b_k

In softmax regression, K is the number of classes (in Chapter 5 it is the number of folds), the probability of class k and the weights and intercept of its score

\boldsymbol\varphi(\mathbf{x})

Feature map: a fixed function from \mathbb{R}^d to \mathbb{R}^p (for example all monomials up to a given degree); models linear in \boldsymbol\varphi are nonlinear in \mathbf{x}

Symbol

Meaning

f,\ f^\ast,\ \mathbf{w}^\ast

The objective to be minimized, its minimum value and a minimizer; the suboptimality is f(\mathbf{w}_k)-f^\ast

\nabla f,\ \nabla^2 f

Gradient (the vector of partial derivatives) and Hessian (the matrix of second derivatives) of f

\eta,\ \eta_k

Step size (learning rate) of gradient descent, constant or at iteration k. (In Chapter 3, \eta(\mathbf{x}) is the regression function.)

L

Smoothness constant: \nabla^2 f\preceq L\mathbf{I}, the largest curvature. (In Chapter 6, L is the log-loss.) L_{\text{glob}} and L_{\text{loc}} are the global bound and the largest curvature at the minimizer

\mu

Strong-convexity constant: \nabla^2 f\succeq\mu\mathbf{I}, the smallest curvature. (Elsewhere \mu is a mean.)

\kappa=L/\mu

Condition number of the problem. (In Chapter 5, \kappa(i) is the fold of example i.)

\rho

Rate of linear convergence: the error is multiplied by at most \rho<1 per iteration

\beta

Momentum parameter of the heavy-ball and Nesterov methods. (In Theorem 7.12, \beta and \gamma are the constants of the step \eta_k=\beta/(\gamma+k).)

B,\ \mathbf{g}_k,\ \sigma^2

Mini-batch size; stochastic gradient at iteration k, unbiased for \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_k); bound on its variance, which for a mini-batch is \sigma^2/B

epoch

One pass over the training set: n/B updates, the cost of one full gradient

\mathbf{M},\ \mathbf{D}

Preconditioner \mathbf{M}=\mathbf{D}\mathbf{D}^\top and the change of variables \mathbf{w}=\mathbf{D}\mathbf{v} it comes from (Proposition 7.7)

\varphi_j(k)

Filter factor of the j-th eigendirection after k gradient steps, 1-(1-\eta h_j)^k, to compare with ridge’s h_j/(h_j+\lambda) (Proposition 7.13)

Symbol

Meaning

y_i\in\{-1,+1\}

Class labels in this chapter and in Section 3.8.4 (Chapter 6 used \{0, 1\} for the logistic regression and \{-1, +1\} only for the signed score m_i)

f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}+b

Score (decision function), with the intercept b kept apart from \mathbf{w} and not penalized; the prediction is \operatorname{sign} f(\mathbf{x})

m_i=y_if(\mathbf{x}_i)

Margin of example i (the signed score of Chapter 6): positive if correct, large if confidently correct. The geometric margin of a hyperplane is \gamma=1/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert when the closest points have m_i=1

\xi_i

Slack variable of example i, \xi_i=\max\{0,1-m_i\} at the optimum

\ell_{\text{hinge}}(m)

Hinge loss \max\{0,1-m\}; \ell_\varepsilon(r)=\max\{0,\lvert r\rvert-\varepsilon\} is the \varepsilon-insensitive loss of support vector regression

C,\ \lambda

Price of a margin violation, and the penalty \lambda=1/(Cn) of the equivalent regularized hinge-loss problem, as in Section 6.5

\alpha_i

Dual variable (Lagrange multiplier) of the constraint of example i; \mathbf{w}=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i. The support vectors are the examples with \alpha_i>0; those with \alpha_i=C are bounded, those with 0<\alpha_i<C free

\mathbf{K},\ k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})

Gram matrix K_{ij}=\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j and its generalization, a kernel k(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j)=\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)^\top\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_j) (Chapter 9). (In Chapter 5, K is the number of folds; in Chapter 6, the number of classes.)

e_t,\ I_{\text{up}},\ I_{\text{low}}

In SMO: e_t=y_t-\sum_s\alpha_sy_sK_{st} and the index sets of the multipliers that can still move up or down (Proposition 8.7)

G

Bound on the norm of the subgradients in Theorem 8.6. (Not to be confused with the gradient G of the dual used in the code of SMO.)

Symbol

Meaning

k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})

Kernel: an inner product in a feature space, k(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})=\langle\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}),\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})\rangle; equivalently a symmetric function whose Gram matrices are positive semidefinite (Theorem 9.1)

\mathbf{K}

Gram (kernel) matrix of the sample, K_{ij}=k(\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{x}_j); \mathbf{K}_{nm}, \mathbf{K}_{mm} are the blocks between the sample and m landmarks, and among the landmarks (Nyström). (In Chapter 5, K is the number of folds; in Chapter 6, the number of classes.)

\gamma

Bandwidth parameter of the Gaussian and Laplacian kernels, \exp(-\gamma\lVert\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{z}\rVert^2); 1/\sqrt\gamma is the length scale. In the polynomial kernel (\gamma\,\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z}+c)^p, \gamma is a scale and c the offset

\mathcal{H}_k,\ \lVert f\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}

Reproducing kernel Hilbert space of k and the norm in it; f(\mathbf{x})=\langle f,k(\cdot,\mathbf{x})\rangle (reproducing property); \lVert f\rVert^2_{\mathcal{H}}=\boldsymbol\alpha^\top\mathbf{K}\boldsymbol\alpha for f=\sum_i\alpha_ik(\cdot,\mathbf{x}_i)

\boldsymbol\alpha

Coefficients of the representer theorem, f=\sum_i\alpha_ik(\cdot,\mathbf{x}_i); for the SVM they are \alpha_iy_i with the multipliers \alpha_i of Chapter 8, for kernel ridge regression (\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y}

\mathbf{H}_\lambda,\ \mu_j

Smoother \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{K}+\lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1} of kernel ridge regression (as in Chapter 6) and the eigenvalues of \mathbf{K}, with \operatorname{df}(\lambda)=\sum_j\mu_j/(\mu_j+\lambda)

\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{x}),\ D

Random Fourier feature map into \mathbb{R}^D (Theorem 9.7). (Not to be confused with the point \mathbf{z} at which a kernel is evaluated.)

Symbol

Meaning

\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_0,\ s

Number of non-zero weights, and the size of a sparse model (Definition 10.1); \mathbf{w}^\ast with s non-zeros is the true weight vector in Sections 10.4 and 10.7

S,\ S^\ast,\ A

A subset of features (a support), the true support, and the active set (the non-zero weights) of the lasso; \mathbf{X}_S is the matrix of the columns in S. (In Chapter 5, S^+,S^- are scores; in Chapter 6, \mathbf{S}=\operatorname{diag}(p_i(1-p_i)); S_t below is a function.)

\mathrm{RSS}, C_p, \mathrm{BIC}

Residual sum of squares of a fit, and the criteria of Section 10.3.2 for choosing the size of a subset: C_p(S)=\mathrm{RSS}(S)/n+2\hat\sigma^2(\lvert S\rvert+1)/n and \mathrm{BIC}(S)=n\ln(\mathrm{RSS}(S)/n)+(\ln n)(\lvert S\rvert+1)

\mathbf{P}_S,\ \mathbf{r},\ \tilde{\mathbf{x}}_j

Orthogonal projection on the span of the columns in S, the current residual, and the part of the feature \mathbf{x}_j orthogonal to that span (Lemma 10.3)

\mu

Mutual coherence of unit-norm features, \max_{i\ne j}\lvert\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j\rvert (Corollary 10.5). (In Chapter 7, \mu is the strong-convexity constant; in Chapter 9, \mu_j are eigenvalues of the Gram matrix.)

\lambda,\ F_\lambda,\ \lambda_{\max}

Lasso penalty in the convention F_\lambda(\mathbf{w})=\frac1{2n}\lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1 (the alpha of scikit-learn), the objective, and the smallest \lambda for which \hat{\mathbf{w}}=\mathbf{0}, \frac1n\lVert\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y}\rVert_\infty (Theorem 10.7). For \ell_1 logistic regression \lambda=1/(nC) (Section 10.9)

S_t(a)

Soft-thresholding operator, \operatorname{sign}(a)\max(\lvert a\rvert-t,0) (Proposition 10.6); also the proximal operator of t\lVert\cdot\rVert_1 (Proposition 10.9)

\lambda_1,\ \lambda_2

Weights of the \ell_1 and the squared \ell_2 penalties of the elastic net, \text{alpha}\cdot\text{l1\_ratio} and \text{alpha}\,(1-\text{l1\_ratio}) in scikit-learn (Definition 10.3)

\rho_{ij}

Correlation of two standardized features, \frac1n\mathbf{z}_i^\top\mathbf{z}_j (Theorem 10.14)

\kappa_S

Condition number of the Hessian of the data term restricted to the support of the solution (Section 10.6.4); explains the linear rate of ISTA after the support is identified

\mathbf{s}_A,\ \boldsymbol\theta,\ \mathbf{u}

Signs of the active weights, and the vectors of Exercise 10.5, with \hat{\mathbf{w}}_A(\lambda)=\boldsymbol\theta-\lambda\mathbf{u} on a segment of the path

Symbol

Meaning

\mathcal{D}

The unknown distribution that generates the data

\mathbb{P}(A)

Probability of the event A

\mathbb{E}[X],\ \operatorname{Var}(X)

Expectation and variance of a random variable

\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)

Gaussian distribution with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2

\mathbb{I}[\cdot]

Indicator function: equal to 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise

Vectors are columns. A vector \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d is a d\times 1 column, and \mathbf{x}^\top is a row.

Indices start at 1 in the mathematics and at 0 in Python. The first sample is \mathbf{x}_1 in the formulas and X[0] in the code. This is a frequent source of off-by-one mistakes.

Code is written in monospace. Names such as X, y, and w match the symbols in the text whenever possible.

Local notation. A chapter may introduce extra symbols for its own purposes. They are defined where they are first used.

Machine learning is usually taught in one of two ways. In the first, it is a collection of recipes: import a model, call fit, call predict, and hope for the best. In the second, it is an abstract theory in which the connection with practice is hard to see. This book sits between the two. It assumes that you already know linear algebra and calculus, and it uses them as the language in which machine learning is explained and then checks every statement with code.

For a reader with that background, most of machine learning is less foreign than it first appears. Ridge regression is a linear system with one small modification. Principal component analysis is the singular value decomposition applied to centered data. Training a neural network is the chain rule applied systematically to a long composition of functions. The aim of this book is to make such connections explicit, to explain the intuition behind each formula, and to let you verify the result on a computer.

The book is written for university students who are starting out in machine learning. It assumes:

Linear algebra: vectors, matrices, dot products, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and the singular value decomposition.

Calculus: derivatives, partial derivatives, gradients, and the chain rule.

No previous knowledge of machine learning is required. Some familiarity with programming helps. Chapter 2 reviews the Python tools used throughout the book (NumPy, pandas, and matplotlib) together with the small amount of probability that the later chapters need. Advanced mathematics, such as measure theory, is not required, and proofs are given only when they help to build intuition.

Every technical chapter is built around the same ingredients:

Learning objectives and intuition, so that you know where the chapter is going and why.

Mathematical formulation and derivations, written step by step in a way that explains each manipulation.

Figures generated by Python code that you can run and modify.

Hands-on implementation on real datasets from standard libraries such as scikit-learn, seaborn, and torchvision.

Worked examples solved both by hand and in code, so that the two can be compared.

Exercises of increasing difficulty, divided into manual (analytical) exercises and Python (computational) exercises. They are meant to be challenging but accessible.

The book follows a practice-first approach. Concepts are introduced together with the code that implements them, and the datasets are real ones. Each chapter is a Jupyter notebook, so you can execute it from beginning to end on your own computer.

The book is organized in five parts.

Part I, Foundations (Chapters 1–3). What machine learning is, how to set up your environment, the Python and probability tools used throughout, and statistical learning theory, the framework that tells us what it means for a model to learn and to generalize.

Part II, Classical Supervised Learning (Chapters 4–11). Nearest-neighbor methods and the bias–variance trade-off, cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning, regularized least squares and logistic regression, stochastic gradient descent, support vector machines, kernels and the representer theorem, sparsity and feature selection (OMP, Lasso, Elastic Net), and decision trees and ensembles.

Part III, Unsupervised Learning (Chapters 12–13). Clustering (k-means, vector quantization, spectral clustering, and how to choose the number of clusters), and dimensionality reduction with SVD, PCA, and kernel PCA.

Part IV, Deep Learning (Chapters 14–21). Neural network fundamentals, backpropagation and the practice of training deep networks, convolutional networks and their applications, recurrent networks (RNN, LSTM, GRU), attention and transformers, autoencoders and GANs, and graph neural networks.

Part V, Decisions and Modern AI (Chapters 22–23). Reinforcement learning with Markov decision processes, Monte Carlo methods, and temporal-difference learning, followed by large language models, modern architectures, AI agents, and future directions.

The book closes with conclusions, appendices (a math cheat sheet, a Python cheat sheet, solutions to the exercises, and a glossary), and a bibliography.

If you are following a full course, read the chapters in order: each one builds on the previous ones. If your main interest is deep learning, a faster route is to read Chapters 1–3 and 5–7, which introduce the setup, the learning framework, evaluation, linear models, and gradient-based optimization, and then to move to Part IV, returning to the classical methods later. In either case, do the exercises: the notebooks are designed to be changed and re-run, and that is where most of the learning happens.

The book aims to be mathematically honest without being heavy. When a result is stated without proof, the text says so and indicates where to find the proof, and the bibliography collects references for readers who want to go further. When a simplification is made for the sake of clarity, it is flagged as such.

This book would not exist without the open-source community. The code is written in Python and runs in Jupyter notebooks. The book is built with Jupyter Book, a project of the Executable Books community. The numerical and learning code relies on NumPy, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, and PyTorch, including its torchvision and torchaudio libraries. Thanks go to the maintainers and contributors of all these projects, and to the researchers and institutions who created and released the open datasets used in the examples; each dataset is cited where it appears.

Mario Medone
